questions.question: Identify the functional group associated with the absorption labelled **A** on the IR spectrum below.
questions.answer: Absorption A is a strong, broad band centred near 3300–3400 cm$^{-1}$, characteristic of an alcohol O–H stretch. There is no strong C=O absorption near 1700 cm$^{-1}$, so C and D are eliminated, and a C–H stretch (just below 3000 cm$^{-1}$) is sharp, not broad.

questions.question:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long been using the ideas of solubility to detoxify foods such as the yellow walnut (*Beilschmiedia bancroftii*).

Identify the method that would best remove water soluble toxins from the yellow walnut.
options: Placing the nuts in a mesh bag in a container of water.
Placing the nuts in a mesh bag in a creek with running water.
Crushing the nuts and placing them in a mesh bag in a container of water.
Crushing the nuts and placing them in a mesh bag in a creek with running water.
questions.answer: Crushing increases the surface area exposed to water, so the toxins dissolve faster. Running water continually removes the dissolved toxin, so the water never becomes saturated and the dissolution equilibrium keeps shifting towards dissolving more toxin.

questions.question:
Magnesium ribbon was combusted in a crucible without a lid until no further reaction was observed. At this point all the shiny, silver coloured magnesium had been converted into magnesium oxide, a white powder.

Based on these observations, this reaction between magnesium and oxygen can be considered
options: a closed system that reached static equilibrium.
an open system that reached static equilibrium.
a closed system that reached dynamic equilibrium.
an open system that reached dynamic equilibrium.
questions.answer: The crucible has no lid, so matter (and energy) can be exchanged with the surroundings: it is an open system. All the magnesium has been converted to product and the reaction has stopped completely (no reverse reaction occurs), so it has reached static equilibrium.

questions.question: Which of the following will a catalyst NOT do when added to an equilibrium reaction?
options: Change the value of the equilibrium constant for the reaction.
Increase the percentage of collisions that result in a reaction.
Increase the rates of both the forward and reverse reactions.
Provide an alternate reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
questions.answer: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and reverse reactions equally, so it speeds both up and a larger fraction of collisions are successful. It does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of $K_{eq}$ (which depends only on temperature).

questions.question:
The table below shows the pH range and colour changes of three indicators.

| Indicator | pH range | Colour range |
|---|---|---|
| Methyl orange | 3.3 – 4.4 | Red to yellow |
| Bromothymol blue | 6.0 – 7.6 | Yellow to blue |
| Phenolphthalein | 8.3 – 10.0 | Colourless to pink |

A student used a pH probe and determined that the pH of a clear, colourless solution was 4.3. She then added each indicator in turn to separate samples of the solution.

Which option correctly identifies the colour of the indicators in the solution (methyl orange / bromothymol blue / phenolphthalein)?
questions.answer: pH 4.3 lies within methyl orange's range (3.3–4.4), so it shows its intermediate colour, orange. pH 4.3 is below 6.0, so bromothymol blue is yellow, and below 8.3, so phenolphthalein is colourless.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the mass spectrum of butanoic acid.

Which of the following m/z corresponds to the base peak?
questions.answer: The base peak is the tallest peak in the spectrum (relative abundance 100), which is at $m/z = 60$. (The molecular ion peak is at $m/z = 88$.)

questions.question:
Consider the following molecule.

What is the systematic name for this compound?
questions.answer: The longest carbon chain has 4 carbons (butane). Numbering from the end nearest the substituents, both the Cl and the methyl group are on C2: 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. Numbering from the other end (option C) gives higher locants; A and D do not describe the longest chain correctly.

questions.question:
A sodium hydroxide solution prepared from analytical-grade NaOH pellets is unsuitable to be used as a primary standard in acid-base titrations.

This is because
options: solutions of sodium hydroxide are colourless.
sodium hydroxide pellets have a low solubility.
sodium hydroxide solutions are caustic and can cause chemical burns.
the exact concentration of the NaOH solution made from the pellets is unknown.
questions.answer: NaOH is hygroscopic (absorbs water from the air) and reacts with atmospheric CO$_2$, so a weighed mass of pellets is not pure NaOH. The exact concentration of the solution is therefore unknown, and it must be standardised before use.

questions.question: Which equation for the reaction between sodium carbonate and dilute hydrochloric acid is correct?
questions.answer: Acid + carbonate $\rightarrow$ salt + water + carbon dioxide. Two Na and two Cl atoms are needed on each side, so 2HCl and 2NaCl; only D is balanced (B has an incorrect formula, Na$_2$Cl).

questions.question: Which of the following combinations correctly identifies the molecular shape around a carbon atom within a carbon-carbon single, double and triple bond (single / double / triple)?
questions.answer: A carbon with only single bonds has four bonding regions (tetrahedral, 109.5°); a carbon in a C=C has three regions (trigonal planar, 120°); a carbon in a C≡C has two regions (linear, 180°).

questions.question:
Consider the following equilibrium system.

$$\text{HS}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{S}^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

Which of the following represents a conjugate acid-base pair in this system?
questions.answer: HS$^-$ donates a proton to water, forming its conjugate base S$^{2-}$. A conjugate pair differs by exactly one H$^+$: HS$^-$/S$^{2-}$ (the other pair is H$_3$O$^+$/H$_2$O).

questions.question:
A strong acid HA completely ionises in aqueous solutions.

1.0 mL of a 1.0 mol/L solution was diluted to 1.00 L with distilled water. 100 mL of this resulting solution was then diluted again to 1.00 L with distilled water.

What is the pH of the final solution?
questions.answer:
First dilution: $c = \dfrac{1.0 \times 0.0010}{1.00} = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.
Second dilution: $c = \dfrac{1.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.100}{1.00} = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$.
HA is fully ionised, so $[\text{H}^+] = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}$ and $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.0 \times 10^{-4}) = 4$.

questions.question: Which option correctly shows the compounds in order of increasing pH?
questions.answer: NH$_4$Cl is an acidic salt ($\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), NaNO$_3$ is neutral (neither ion hydrolyses), and Na$_2$CO$_3$ is basic ($\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{OH}^-$). Increasing pH: NH$_4$Cl < NaNO$_3$ < Na$_2$CO$_3$.

questions.question:
This apparatus was set up to produce an ester with molecular formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_2$.

The ester was formed by refluxing propan-2-ol and a suitable carboxylic acid in the presence of an acid catalyst.

Identify the structure of this ester.
questions.answer: Carboxylic acid + alcohol $\rightarrow$ ester + water, with the alcohol's carbon chain bonded to the single-bonded O of the ester. Propan-2-ol contributes an isopropyl group, $-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$, on the O. To make C$_6$ in total the acid must be propanoic acid (C$_3$). Only B (propan-2-yl propanoate, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$) has a branched isopropyl group attached to the O.

questions.question:
A sealed glass tube contains an equilibrium mixture of brown nitrogen dioxide gas, NO$_2$, and colourless dinitrogen tetroxide gas, N$_2$O$_4$.

$$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)$$

At time $t_1$ the temperature of the mixture is increased. The graph shows the gas concentrations over time.

Identify the correct statement.
options: The reaction as written is endothermic AND the $K_{eq}$ increases after $t_1$.
The reaction as written is exothermic AND the $K_{eq}$ increases after $t_1$.
The reaction as written is endothermic AND the $K_{eq}$ decreases after $t_1$.
The reaction as written is exothermic AND the $K_{eq}$ decreases after $t_1$.
questions.answer:
After the temperature increase, [NO$_2$] falls and [N$_2$O$_4$] rises, so the equilibrium shifted left. By Le Chatelier's principle, heating favours the endothermic direction, so the reverse reaction is endothermic and the forward reaction (as written) is exothermic. With less product and more reactant, $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]^2}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]}$ decreases.

*Note: the answer follows the graph given. For the real system, N$_2$O$_4 \rightarrow$ 2NO$_2$ is endothermic, and heating it makes the mixture browner.*

questions.question: Which of the following titration curves represents NaOH being added to an acidic buffer solution?
questions.answer: An acidic buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base. Adding strong base gives a weak acid–strong base titration curve: the pH starts low and rises only slowly through the buffer region, then rises sharply at the equivalence point before levelling off at high pH. This is curve C. Curves B and D show pH falling, which cannot happen when base is added. Curve A has no buffer region.

questions.question:
In the upper atmosphere, oxygen gas (O$_2$) and ozone gas (O$_3$) are in equilibrium at a particular temperature with $K_{eq} = 8 \times 10^{-24}$.

$$3\text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{O}_3(g)$$

If $[\text{O}_2(g)]$ at this temperature is $2 \times 10^{-3}$ M and $[\text{O}_3(g)]$ is $4 \times 10^{-6}$ M, the reaction would be
questions.answer:
$$Q = \frac{[\text{O}_3]^2}{[\text{O}_2]^3} = \frac{(4 \times 10^{-6})^2}{(2 \times 10^{-3})^3} = \frac{1.6 \times 10^{-11}}{8 \times 10^{-9}} = 2 \times 10^{-3}$$
$Q \gg K_{eq}$ ($2 \times 10^{-3} > 8 \times 10^{-24}$), so there is too much product. The reverse reaction is favoured until $Q$ falls to $K_{eq}$.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of solutions, upon mixing, will produce the solution with the highest temperature change?
options: 200 mL 0.10 M NaOH$(aq)$ + 100 mL 0.25 M HNO$_3(aq)$
100 mL 0.10 M NaOH$(aq)$ + 100 mL 0.10 M CH$_3$COOH$(aq)$
100 mL 0.40 M NaOH$(aq)$ + 50 mL 1.0 M HNO$_3(aq)$
questions.answer:
$\Delta T \propto$ (moles of water formed) / (total mass of solution). Moles of water formed = moles of the limiting reagent:

- A: $n(\text{OH}^-) = 0.020$, $n(\text{H}^+) = 0.025$; 0.020 mol in 300 mL $\Rightarrow 0.067$ mol L$^{-1}$
- B: 0.010 mol in 200 mL $\Rightarrow 0.050$ mol L$^{-1}$, and a weak acid releases less heat (energy is used to ionise it)
- C: $n(\text{OH}^-) = 0.010$, $n(\text{H}^+) = 0.020$; 0.010 mol in 150 mL $\Rightarrow 0.067$ mol L$^{-1}$
- D: $n(\text{OH}^-) = 0.040$, $n(\text{H}^+) = 0.050$; 0.040 mol in 150 mL $\Rightarrow 0.27$ mol L$^{-1}$

D releases the most heat per unit mass of solution, so it gives the largest temperature change.

questions.question: How many alcohols are structural isomers with the formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH}$?
questions.answer: Butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. That makes 4 alcohols. (Ethers such as diethyl ether have the same molecular formula but are not alcohols.)

questions.question:
The table lists some properties of the carbon compounds W, X, Y and Z.

| Compound | Reactivity with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7/\text{H}^+$ | Solubility in water |
|---|---|---|
| W | Solution turns green | Insoluble |
| X | Orange colour remains | Insoluble |
| Y | Solution turns green | Soluble |
| Z | Orange colour remains | Soluble |

Which option best identifies the compounds W, X, Y and Z (in that order)?
questions.answer:
Acidified dichromate (orange) is reduced to green Cr$^{3+}$ by primary and secondary alcohols; tertiary alcohols and alkanes are not oxidised, so the solution stays orange.
- Not oxidised (X, Z): ethane and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The alkane is insoluble (X = C$_2$H$_6$); the small tertiary alcohol is soluble (Z = (CH$_3$)$_3$COH).
- Oxidised (W, Y): hexan-1-ol has a long non-polar chain and is insoluble (W); propan-2-ol is small and soluble (Y).

This matches B.

questions.question:
The apparatus shown was set up to heat water using a methanol spirit burner.

Assuming complete combustion and that there is no heat loss to the surroundings, calculate the final temperature of the water using the data provided in the table. (Specific heat capacity of water $= 4.18$ J g$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.)

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass of water heated (g) | 200.0 |
| Initial temperature of water (°C) | 17.5 |
| Molar heat of combustion of methanol (kJ/mol) | $-726$ |
| Mass of methanol used (g) | 2.82 |
questions.answer:
$M(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}) = 12.01 + 4(1.008) + 16.00 = 32.042$ g mol$^{-1}$

$$n(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}) = \frac{m}{M} = \frac{2.82}{32.042} = 0.08801 \text{ mol}$$

Heat released (all absorbed by the water):
$$q = n \times |\Delta H_c| = 0.08801 \times 726 \times 10^{3} = 6.389 \times 10^{4} \text{ J}$$

Using $q = mc\Delta T$:
$$\Delta T = \frac{q}{mc} = \frac{6.389 \times 10^{4}}{200.0 \times 4.18} = 76.4\ \text{K}$$

$$T_f = T_i + \Delta T = 17.5 + 76.4 = 93.9\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

questions.question:
Soap is used to clean a range of items in our everyday life. The diagram shows the first step (Step 1) in the removal of grease from a surface using soapy water: soap anions dissolved in the water near a drop of grease on a surface.

Construct diagrams to show the remaining steps (Step 2 and Step 3) in this process and explain how soap removes grease from a surface.
questions.answer:
**Diagrams:**
- *Step 2:* soap anions drawn with their long non-polar hydrocarbon tails embedded in the grease and their charged carboxylate heads ($-\text{COO}^-$) pointing out into the water.
- *Step 3:* the grease lifted off the surface as a **micelle**: a sphere of grease surrounded by soap anions, with tails inside the grease and the negative heads on the outside, suspended in water.

**Explanation:** In Step 1 the soap anions are dissolved in the water. In Step 2, the hydrophobic (non-polar) hydrocarbon tails of the soap anions are attracted to the non-polar grease by dispersion forces and embed themselves in it, while the hydrophilic (polar, negatively charged) heads stay in the water, forming ion–dipole forces with water molecules. As more soap anions attach and the mixture is agitated, the grease is broken into small droplets and lifted from the surface, forming micelles: grease in the centre, surrounded by the non-polar tails, with the anionic heads facing outwards. The negatively charged surfaces of the micelles repel each other, so the droplets do not join up again and stay suspended (emulsified) in the water. In Step 3, the micelles are rinsed away with the water, so the grease is removed from the surface.

questions.question:
According to the Arrhenius theory of acids and bases, sodium acetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) is an example of a salt, yet according to the more modern Brønsted–Lowry theory it is an example of a base.

Justify the above statement, supporting your response with a relevant balanced equation.
questions.answer:
**Arrhenius:** an Arrhenius acid produces H$^+$ in water and an Arrhenius base produces OH$^-$; acid + base $\rightarrow$ salt + water. Sodium acetate is the salt formed when acetic acid (an Arrhenius acid) is neutralised by sodium hydroxide (an Arrhenius base):
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COONa}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
It does not itself contain OH$^-$, so Arrhenius classifies it only as a salt.

**Brønsted–Lowry:** a base is a proton (H$^+$) acceptor. When sodium acetate dissolves it forms Na$^+$ and CH$_3$COO$^-$ ions. The acetate ion accepts a proton from water, producing hydroxide ions, so the solution is basic and acetate acts as a base:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$

The Brønsted–Lowry definition is based on proton transfer rather than on the substance containing OH$^-$, so it can classify the acetate ion as a base.

questions.question:
A student has discovered four unlabelled bottles in the laboratory. Each bottle contains an aqueous solution of ONE of the following: barium nitrate, calcium nitrate, magnesium nitrate, silver nitrate.

Draw a flow chart to show a sequence of tests that could be performed in a school laboratory to distinguish the cation present within each solution.

The available materials are: 1 M NaOH$(aq)$, 1 M HCl$(aq)$, 1 M H$_2$SO$_4(aq)$, wire loop and Bunsen burner.

Include expected observations and ONE net ionic equation.
questions.answer:
**Flow chart (test a fresh sample of each unknown):**

1. **Add 1 M HCl$(aq)$.**
   - White precipitate (AgCl) $\rightarrow$ **Ag$^+$** (silver nitrate).
   - No precipitate $\rightarrow$ Ba$^{2+}$, Ca$^{2+}$ or Mg$^{2+}$: go to step 2.
2. **To a new sample, add 1 M H$_2$SO$_4(aq)$.**
   - No precipitate $\rightarrow$ **Mg$^{2+}$** (magnesium nitrate). This can be confirmed by adding 1 M NaOH: a white precipitate of Mg(OH)$_2$ forms.
   - White precipitate (BaSO$_4$ or CaSO$_4$) $\rightarrow$ Ba$^{2+}$ or Ca$^{2+}$: go to step 3.
3. **Flame test** (dip a clean wire loop into the solution and hold it in a blue Bunsen flame).
   - Brick-red / orange-red flame $\rightarrow$ **Ca$^{2+}$** (calcium nitrate).
   - Pale apple-green flame $\rightarrow$ **Ba$^{2+}$** (barium nitrate).

**Net ionic equation** (any one), e.g.
$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s)$$
(or $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$, or $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$)

questions.question:
As the effects of the uses of fossil fuels become more apparent, there has been a move to use renewable fuels such as bioethanol.

The equations below show the complete combustion of octane and bioethanol.

Complete combustion of octane, the main component of petrol:
$$\text{C}_8\text{H}_{18}(l) + \tfrac{25}{2}\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 8\text{CO}_2(g) + 9\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad \Delta H_c = -5470 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Complete combustion of ethanol:
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(l) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \qquad \Delta H_c = -1370 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Compare the use of petrol and bioethanol as fuels, including the environmental impacts of each. Make use of the information above in your response.
questions.answer:
**Energy released:** octane has a much larger molar heat of combustion ($-5470$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) than ethanol ($-1370$ kJ mol$^{-1}$), so about four times as many moles of ethanol must be burnt to release the same energy. Per gram the difference is smaller (octane $\approx 47.9$ kJ g$^{-1}$, ethanol $\approx 29.7$ kJ g$^{-1}$), but petrol still delivers more energy per litre, so a vehicle needs a larger volume of bioethanol to travel the same distance.

**Completeness of combustion:** ethanol already contains oxygen and needs only 3 mol O$_2$ per mole, compared with 12.5 mol O$_2$ per mole of octane. Ethanol therefore burns more completely and cleanly, producing less soot (C) and toxic carbon monoxide (CO), so there is less harmful air pollution than with petrol.

**Greenhouse gases:** each mole of ethanol burnt produces 2 mol CO$_2$ compared with 8 mol for octane. More importantly, bioethanol is made by fermenting crops (e.g. sugar cane) that absorbed CO$_2$ by photosynthesis while growing, so it is close to carbon neutral (apart from CO$_2$ released when farming, fermenting and distilling it). The CO$_2$ from petrol comes from carbon that was locked away underground, so it adds to the atmosphere and makes the enhanced greenhouse effect and climate change worse.

**Sustainability:** bioethanol is renewable because crops can be regrown quickly, whereas petrol comes from crude oil, which is non-renewable. However, growing fuel crops uses land, water and fertiliser that could be used for food.

**Overall:** petrol releases more energy per mole and per gram, but bioethanol has a smaller environmental impact because it burns more cleanly, is renewable and gives a much lower net CO$_2$ output.

questions.question:
The table lists the pH of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions of four different acids at 25 °C.

| Acid | pH |
|---|---|
| A | 1.0 |
| B | 2.9 |
| C | 0.7 |
| D | 2.1 |

Three of the acids are monoprotic; the fourth contains more than one acidic hydrogen.

Which of A, B, C or D must be the acid with more than one acidic hydrogen? Justify your choice.
questions.answer:
**Acid C.**

A 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ monoprotic acid can produce at most $[\text{H}^+] = 0.10$ mol L$^{-1}$, even if it is strong and fully ionised. This gives a minimum pH of $-\log_{10}(0.10) = 1.0$ (as for acid A). Acid C has pH 0.7, so
$$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-0.7} = 0.20 \text{ mol L}^{-1} > 0.10 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$
Each molecule must therefore release more than one H$^+$, so C must have more than one acidic hydrogen (e.g. H$_2$SO$_4$). Acids B and D have pH above 1.0, which is consistent with weak monoprotic acids.

questions.question:
Methanoic acid (HCOOH) is a monoprotic weak acid. A 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of methanoic acid has a pH of 2.1 at 25 °C.

Calculate the $K_a$ of methanoic acid.
questions.answer:
$$\text{HCOOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCOO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \qquad K_a = \frac{[\text{HCOO}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{HCOOH}]}$$

$[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-2.1} = 7.943 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

From the 1:1 ratio in the equation, $[\text{HCOO}^-] = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 7.943 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

At equilibrium, $[\text{HCOOH}] = 0.10 - 7.943 \times 10^{-3} = 0.0921$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$K_a = \frac{(7.943 \times 10^{-3})^2}{0.0921} = 6.9 \times 10^{-4}$$

questions.question:
Consider the solubility in water of the following organic compounds.

| Compound | Molecular mass (g/mol) | Solubility in water (g/100 mL) |
|---|---|---|
| Propan-2-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHOHCH}_3$ | 60.10 | 100 |
| Propanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ | 58.08 | 5 |
| Butane, $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}$ | 58.12 | 0.0061 |

Explain the difference in the solubility in water of the three organic compounds. Include one relevant diagram as part of your response.
questions.answer:
The three compounds have almost the same molar mass, so the differences in solubility are caused by the different intermolecular forces each can form with water.

**Propan-2-ol** is the most soluble (100 g/100 mL, i.e. miscible). Its hydroxyl group is both a hydrogen-bond donor (the O–H hydrogen) and an acceptor (two lone pairs on O), so each molecule can form up to three hydrogen bonds with water molecules. These strong, extensive hydrogen bonds with water replace the hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Its non-polar part is small (two methyl groups).

**Propanal** is much less soluble (5 g/100 mL). Its carbonyl oxygen can accept hydrogen bonds from water, but propanal has no O–H hydrogen to donate, so it forms fewer hydrogen bonds with water (otherwise only dipole–dipole forces). It also has a relatively larger non-polar ethyl region, which disrupts the hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

**Butane** is almost insoluble (0.0061 g/100 mL). It is non-polar and can form only weak dispersion forces with water. These are far weaker than the hydrogen bonds between water molecules that would have to be broken, so very little dissolves.

**Diagram:** a propan-2-ol molecule with dashed hydrogen bonds from its O–H hydrogen to the O of a water molecule and from two water H atoms to the lone pairs on its O, labelled with $\delta^+$/$\delta^-$ (see below). Compare propanal, which can only accept hydrogen bonds at its C=O oxygen.

questions.question:
A student mixes 25.0 mL of 0.020 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium carbonate with 125.0 mL of $3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ barium nitrate solution.

Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + \text{Ba(NO}_3)_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaCO}_3(s) + 2\text{NaNO}_3(aq)$$

questions.question:
A student mixes 25.0 mL of 0.020 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium carbonate with 125.0 mL of $3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$ barium nitrate solution.

Determine whether the student will observe a precipitate of barium carbonate form when the two solutions are mixed together. ($K_{sp}(\text{BaCO}_3) = 2.58 \times 10^{-9}$)
questions.answer:
$$\text{BaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = 2.58 \times 10^{-9}$$

Total volume after mixing $= 25.0 + 125.0 = 150.0$ mL.

$[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = \dfrac{c_1V_1}{V_2} = \dfrac{0.020 \times 0.0250}{0.1500} = 3.3 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

$[\text{Ba}^{2+}] = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.1250}{0.1500} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$

$$Q = [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = (2.5 \times 10^{-4})(3.3 \times 10^{-3}) = 8.3 \times 10^{-7}$$

$Q > K_{sp}$ ($8.3 \times 10^{-7} > 2.58 \times 10^{-9}$), so the solution is supersaturated and a white precipitate of BaCO$_3$ **will** form.

questions.question:
Conductivity curves show the change in the electrical conductivity during a titration and can be used to determine the equivalence point of a reaction.

The curve shows the change in conductivity upon the addition of aqueous ammonia solution to nitric acid.

Which letter A – C most closely shows the equivalence point for the reaction?
questions.answer: **B.** The conductivity reaches its minimum at B, where all the H$^+$ ions from the nitric acid have just been neutralised; after B the slope of the graph changes.

questions.question:
Conductivity curves show the change in the electrical conductivity during a titration and can be used to determine the equivalence point of a reaction.

The curve shows the change in conductivity upon the addition of aqueous ammonia solution to nitric acid.

Account for the shape of the curve, using all the letters in your response.
questions.answer:
**A:** the initial conductivity is high because HNO$_3$ is a strong acid that is fully ionised, so the solution contains a high concentration of mobile H$_3$O$^+$ and NO$_3^-$ ions. H$_3$O$^+$ ions are especially good conductors.

**A to B:** as ammonia is added it neutralises the acid:
$$\text{NH}_3(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
The highly conductive H$_3$O$^+$ ions are replaced by less mobile NH$_4^+$ ions (and diluted), so the conductivity falls steadily. It reaches a minimum at B, the equivalence point, where all the H$_3$O$^+$ has been neutralised and the solution contains only NH$_4^+$ and NO$_3^-$.

**B to C:** after the equivalence point, extra ammonia is added. NH$_3$ is a weak base that only partially ionises ($\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$), and this ionisation is further suppressed by the NH$_4^+$ already present (common-ion effect). Very few extra ions are formed, so the conductivity rises only slightly and the line is almost flat.

questions.question:
When hydrogen and carbon monoxide are added to a container at 430 °C the following equilibrium system is obtained.

$$2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$$

Write the equilibrium expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]}{[\text{H}_2]^2[\text{CO}]}$$

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium
$$2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$$

0.045 mol hydrogen and 0.080 mol carbon monoxide are added to a 1.00 L container at 430 °C and allowed to reach equilibrium. At equilibrium the amount of methanol is 0.011 mol.

Calculate the equilibrium constant for the system.

Consider the equilibrium
$$2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$$

Using Le Chatelier's Principle, explain the effect of decreasing the volume of the container on the methanol concentration.
questions.answer: Decreasing the volume increases the concentration of all the gases, so the total pressure increases. According to Le Chatelier's principle, the system shifts to partially counteract this change by reducing the pressure, i.e. towards the side with fewer moles of gas. There are 3 mol of gas on the reactant side (2 H$_2$ + 1 CO) and 1 mol on the product side, so the equilibrium shifts to the right (forward reaction favoured). More methanol is produced, so $[\text{CH}_3\text{OH}]$ increases.

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium
$$2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$$

At time = 20 seconds hydrogen was added to the equilibrium mixture. Using collision theory, account for the shape of the rate–time graph for the **forward** reaction, from 20 seconds until equilibrium is re-established.
questions.answer:
**Sharp increase at 20 s:** adding H$_2$ suddenly increases [H$_2$]. With more reactant particles per unit volume, the frequency of collisions between H$_2$ and CO molecules increases, so the frequency of successful collisions increases and the forward rate rises immediately (vertical jump in the graph).

**Gradual decrease:** the forward rate is now greater than the reverse rate, so there is a net forward reaction. H$_2$ and CO are used up faster than they are re-formed, so [H$_2$] and [CO] gradually decrease. This means fewer collisions, and fewer successful collisions, per second between reactant particles, so the forward rate decreases (the curve slopes down). At the same time [CH$_3$OH] increases, so the reverse rate rises.

**Plateau:** when the forward and reverse rates become equal, equilibrium is re-established. The concentrations, and so the frequency of successful collisions, become constant, and the forward rate levels off. The new constant rate is higher than the original, because [H$_2$] is still higher than before the addition.

questions.question:
A student adds 75.0 mL of 0.15 M sodium hydroxide to 50.0 mL of 0.10 M sulfuric acid.

Calculate the pH of the solution after the chemical reaction has occurred.
questions.answer:
$$2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

$n(\text{NaOH}) = cV = 0.15 \times 0.0750 = 0.01125$ mol

$n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 0.10 \times 0.0500 = 0.00500$ mol

NaOH : H$_2$SO$_4$ = 2 : 1, so NaOH needed $= 2 \times 0.00500 = 0.0100$ mol. H$_2$SO$_4$ is limiting and NaOH is in excess.

$n(\text{OH}^-)_{\text{excess}} = 0.01125 - 0.0100 = 0.00125$ mol

Total volume $= 75.0 + 50.0 = 125.0$ mL $= 0.1250$ L

$$[\text{OH}^-] = \frac{0.00125}{0.1250} = 0.0100 \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$

$\text{pOH} = -\log_{10}(0.0100) = 2.00$, so $\text{pH} = 14.00 - 2.00 = 12.00$.

questions.question:
A reaction pathway to synthesise *N*-ethylpropanamide is shown in the flow chart. Compound A reacts with H$_2$O/H$^+$ to form compound B, which is oxidised by Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$/H$^+$ (strong oxidant) to compound D. Ethene reacts with HCl to form compound C, which reacts with NH$_3$ to form ethanamine. Compound D and ethanamine are refluxed together to form *N*-ethylpropanamide.

Complete the flow chart by drawing the structural formulae for *N*-ethylpropanamide and compounds A, B, C and D.
questions.answer:
Work backwards from the product. *N*-ethylpropanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, is a condensation product of ethanamine and propanoic acid, so D is propanoic acid. D is made by strong oxidation of a primary alcohol, so B is propan-1-ol. B is made by hydration of an alkene, so A is propene.

- **Compound A:** propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}{=}\text{CH}_2$
- **Compound B:** propan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$
- **Compound D:** propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$
- **Compound C:** chloroethane, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ (from addition of HCl to ethene); this then undergoes substitution with NH$_3$ to give ethanamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$
- **N-ethylpropanamide:** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}({=}\text{O})\text{NHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, formed with water:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

All structures should be drawn in full structural form (see the completed flow chart below).

*Note: hydrating propene gives mainly propan-2-ol (which would oxidise to propanone), with propan-1-ol as the minor product. The pathway needs propan-1-ol, which is the answer the marking scheme expects.*

questions.question:
A 1.32 g sample of impure magnesium metal was analysed by allowing it to react with 100.0 mL of 0.750 mol/L HCl$(aq)$. The remaining solution is titrated with 0.250 mol/L NaOH$(aq)$, and the average titre volume is 45.00 mL.

Assuming the impurities do not react with the acid, calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium in the sample.
questions.answer:
$$\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)$$
$$\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

Initial $n(\text{HCl}) = 0.750 \times 0.1000 = 0.0750$ mol

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.250 \times 0.04500 = 0.01125$ mol $= n(\text{HCl})_{\text{excess}}$ (1 : 1 ratio)

$n(\text{HCl})_{\text{reacted with Mg}} = 0.0750 - 0.01125 = 0.06375$ mol

$n(\text{Mg}) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 0.06375 = 0.031875$ mol (Mg : HCl = 1 : 2)

$m(\text{Mg}) = 0.031875 \times 24.31 = 0.7749$ g

$$\%\text{Mg} = \frac{0.7749}{1.32} \times 100 = 58.7\%$$

questions.question:
A textbook states that 'the molar solubility of silver carbonate is higher in water than it is in a 0.100 M silver nitrate solution'.

Justify that the statement is correct using calculations AND Le Chatelier's Principle. ($K_{sp}(\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3) = 8.46 \times 10^{-12}$)
questions.answer:
$$\text{Ag}_2\text{CO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{CO}_3^{2-}(aq) \qquad K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+]^2[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = 8.46 \times 10^{-12}$$

**In water:** let the molar solubility be $x$. Then $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = x$ and $[\text{Ag}^+] = 2x$ (2 : 1 ratio).
$$K_{sp} = (2x)^2(x) = 4x^3 = 8.46 \times 10^{-12} \Rightarrow x = \sqrt[3]{\frac{8.46 \times 10^{-12}}{4}} = 1.28 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$

**In 0.100 M AgNO$_3$:** let the molar solubility be $x$, so $[\text{CO}_3^{2-}] = x$ and $[\text{Ag}^+] = 0.100 + 2x$.

| | $\text{Ag}^+$ | $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.100 | 0 |
| Change | $+2x$ | $+x$ |
| Equilibrium | $0.100 + 2x$ | $x$ |

Because $K_{sp}$ is very small, $x \ll 0.100$, so $0.100 + 2x \approx 0.100$:
$$8.46 \times 10^{-12} = (0.100)^2 x \Rightarrow x = \frac{8.46 \times 10^{-12}}{0.0100} = 8.46 \times 10^{-10} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$
(The assumption is valid: $2x = 1.7 \times 10^{-9} \ll 0.100$.)

**Conclusion from the calculations:** the molar solubility in 0.100 M AgNO$_3$ ($8.46 \times 10^{-10}$ mol L$^{-1}$) is much lower than in water ($1.28 \times 10^{-4}$ mol L$^{-1}$), so the statement is correct.

**Le Chatelier's principle:** silver nitrate is fully soluble and supplies a high concentration of Ag$^+$, an ion that also appears in the dissolution equilibrium (common-ion effect). The higher [Ag$^+$] is a disturbance, so the equilibrium shifts left to reduce [Ag$^+$]. More solid Ag$_2$CO$_3$ forms and less dissolves, so the molar solubility of silver carbonate is lower in the AgNO$_3$ solution than in pure water.

questions.question:
A synthetic medicinal chemist isolated and purified an organic product from a series of reactions which had been designed to produce a brominated organic compound. Bromine can be present as $^{79}$Br and $^{81}$Br.

The chemist obtained the following spectral data (mass spectrum, IR spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR spectrum and $^{1}$H NMR spectrum) of the purified product to determine the structure of the molecule. Highlighted (grey) features: the M$^{+}$ peaks at $m/z$ 152/154; the broad IR absorption at 3400–2400 cm$^{-1}$ (and the strong absorption at 1696 cm$^{-1}$); the $^{13}$C peak near 172 ppm; and the two 2H signals near 3.0 and 3.6 ppm in the $^1$H NMR, shown expanded in the inset. The $^1$H NMR also shows a 1H signal near 11.8 ppm.

Deduce the structural formula of the molecule consistent with the spectra provided. Identify the IUPAC name of the proposed structure and relate the highlighted features of the spectra to the structure.
questions.answer:
**Structure:** $\text{Br}{-}\text{CH}_2{-}\text{CH}_2{-}\text{COOH}$   **IUPAC name: 3-bromopropanoic acid**

**Mass spectrum**
- Two molecular ion peaks of about equal height at $m/z$ 152 and 154. They differ by 2 mass units because of the two bromine isotopes ($^{79}$Br and $^{81}$Br are about equally abundant), so the molecule contains **one** Br atom. $M = 152$ fits C$_3$H$_5$$^{79}$BrO$_2$ ($36 + 5 + 79 + 32 = 152$).
- $m/z$ 107/109 $= [\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}]^+$ (with $^{79}$Br/$^{81}$Br); $m/z$ 73 (base peak) $= [\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}]^+$, from loss of Br; $m/z$ 45 $= [\text{COOH}]^+$.

**IR spectrum**
- Very broad absorption from 3400 to 2400 cm$^{-1}$: O–H stretch of a carboxylic acid (hydrogen-bonded).
- Strong, sharp absorption at 1696 cm$^{-1}$: C=O stretch. Together these show a $-\text{COOH}$ group.

**$^{13}$C NMR spectrum**
- Three peaks, so there are three different carbon environments (3 carbons).
- $\delta \approx 172$ ppm: the C=O carbon of a carboxylic acid.
- Two peaks in the 20–40 ppm region (about 37 and 26 ppm): two different sp$^3$ CH$_2$ carbons, one next to the COOH group and one bonded to Br.

**$^{1}$H NMR spectrum** (5 H in 3 environments, ratio 1 : 2 : 2)
- $\delta \approx 11.8$ ppm, 1H singlet: the carboxylic acid $-\text{COOH}$ proton.
- $\delta \approx 3.6$ ppm, 2H triplet: $-\text{CH}_2-$ bonded to Br (strongly deshielded by the electronegative Br). It is split into a triplet by the 2 H on the neighbouring CH$_2$ ($n + 1 = 3$).
- $\delta \approx 3.0$ ppm, 2H triplet: $-\text{CH}_2-$ next to the C=O, split into a triplet by the neighbouring CH$_2$.
- Two triplets of 2H each show two adjacent CH$_2$ groups, $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$, with no other H neighbours. One end is bonded to Br and the other to COOH.

**Putting it together:** one Br, a COOH group, and a $-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2-$ unit joining them gives Br–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–COOH, 3-bromopropanoic acid. (The isomer 2-bromopropanoic acid, CH$_3$CHBrCOOH, is ruled out because it would give a 3H doublet and a 1H quartet.)

*Note: the paper's sample answer quotes the two CH$_2$ carbons at δ 45 and 35 ppm; the spectrum provided shows them at about 37 and 26 ppm. The conclusion is unchanged.*

questions.question:
*AbbPharm* produces a multivitamin which includes a range of vitamins and minerals. Each multivitamin tablet contains the following minerals:

| Mineral | Mass in tablet (mg) |
|---|---|
| Calcium (394 mg as calcium carbonate and 6 mg as calcium hydrogen phosphate) | 400 |
| Magnesium (as magnesium oxide) | 64.0 |
| Iron (as ferrous fumarate) | 6.8 |
| Zinc (as zinc oxide) | 0.21 |
| Chromium (as chromic chloride hexahydrate) | 0.025 |
| Copper (as cupric sulfate) | 0.900 |
| Iodine (as potassium iodide) | 0.150 |

A laboratory was asked to determine the mass of zinc in the *AbbPharm* multivitamin. A chemist carried out two methods.

**Method 1: Gravimetric analysis.** The chemist took 4 multivitamin tablets, ground them up individually, and dissolved them in 10% nitric acid. Excess 1.0 M NaOH was added to each tablet. The resulting precipitates were dried to constant mass and then weighed. The mean mass of the precipitate formed was 9.20 mg.

**Method 2: Atomic absorption spectroscopy.** The chemist prepared 4 tablet samples for analysis by dissolving the tablets individually in 10% nitric acid. Each tablet solution was made up to a final volume of 100.0 mL. Five standard solutions of zinc were also prepared. The absorbances of the standard and sample solutions were determined by AAS at 213.9 nm.

| Standard Zn$^{2+}$ solution (mg L$^{-1}$) | Absorbance |
|---|---|
| 0.00 | 0.000 |
| 1.00 | 0.170 |
| 2.00 | 0.330 |
| 3.00 | 0.503 |
| 4.00 | 0.680 |

The mean absorbance of the tablet solution was 0.280.

Draw a calibration graph from the AAS data, and evaluate the TWO methods in their validity for determining the mass of zinc in the tablets. Include at least one relevant equation and one calculation in your answer.
questions.answer:
**Calibration graph:** plot absorbance ($y$-axis) against [Zn$^{2+}$] in mg L$^{-1}$ ($x$-axis) for the five standards and draw a straight line of best fit through the origin (gradient $\approx 0.17$ L mg$^{-1}$). The line shows absorbance is directly proportional to concentration in this range.

**Method 2 – AAS:** reading across from $A = 0.280$ to the line and down gives [Zn$^{2+}$] $\approx 1.65$ mg L$^{-1}$ (this is within the range of the standards).
$$m(\text{Zn}) = 1.65 \text{ mg L}^{-1} \times 0.1000 \text{ L} = 0.165 \text{ mg per tablet}$$
(As ZnO: $n = \dfrac{0.165 \times 10^{-3}}{65.38} = 2.52 \times 10^{-6}$ mol, so $m(\text{ZnO}) = 2.52 \times 10^{-6} \times 81.38 = 0.205$ mg.) This is reasonably close to the 0.21 mg stated on the label.

AAS is a **valid** method. The zinc hollow-cathode lamp emits light at 213.9 nm, a wavelength absorbed only by zinc atoms, so the other metals in the tablet (Ca, Mg, Fe, Cu, Cr) do not interfere and only zinc is measured. AAS is sensitive enough to measure the very small amount of zinc (sub-milligram) accurately. A calibration curve with five standards is used, the sample absorbance lies within the calibration range, and four tablets were tested, which improves reliability.

**Method 1 – Gravimetric analysis:** the intended reaction is
$$\text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn(OH)}_2(s)$$
If the precipitate were all Zn(OH)$_2$ ($M = 99.40$ g mol$^{-1}$):
$$n = \frac{9.20 \times 10^{-3}}{99.40} = 9.26 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol}, \quad m(\text{Zn}) = 9.26 \times 10^{-5} \times 65.38 = 6.05 \text{ mg}$$
(equivalent to 7.53 mg ZnO). This is about 30 times the stated 0.21 mg.

This method is **not valid**, because it does not measure only zinc. Excess NaOH also precipitates the other cations in the tablet, e.g. $\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$, along with Fe(OH)$_2$/Fe(OH)$_3$, Cu(OH)$_2$, Cr(OH)$_3$ and some Ca(OH)$_2$. The precipitate is therefore a mixture and its mass is much greater than the mass of Zn(OH)$_2$ alone. In addition, Zn(OH)$_2$ is amphoteric and redissolves in excess NaOH (forming zincate ions), and the tiny mass of Zn(OH)$_2$ expected (about 0.3 mg per tablet) is too small to weigh accurately on a laboratory balance.

**Judgement:** AAS is a valid method for determining the mass of zinc in the tablets (about 0.17 mg Zn per tablet, consistent with the label). Gravimetric analysis with NaOH is not valid for this sample.

questions.question:
The following diagrams represent samples of four acids (key: filled circle = H$^+$, open circle = acid anion, joined filled + open circles = undissociated (unionised) acid).

Which beaker contains a concentrated, weak acid?
questions.answer: A weak acid is only partially ionised, so most of the acid is present as undissociated molecules; a concentrated acid has many acid particles per unit volume. Beaker W contains many particles, most of them undissociated acid with only a few H$^+$ and anion particles, so it is a concentrated weak acid. (V is concentrated but fully ionised — strong; T is a dilute strong acid; U is a dilute weak acid.)

questions.question: What type of reaction is the conversion of ethene into ethane?
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CH}_2 + \text{H}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3$ (Pt/Ni catalyst): adding H$_2$ across the double bond is hydrogenation.

questions.question: What is the name of the compound shown?
questions.answer: The chain has 3 carbons (propane). Numbering from the end carrying the halogens gives Cl and F on C1 and F on C2 (lowest locants 1,1,2). Substituents are listed alphabetically (chloro before fluoro): 1-chloro-1,2-difluoropropane.

questions.question: Which of the following are isomers?
questions.answer: Isomers have the same molecular formula. Methyl ethanoate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_3$) and propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) are both $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}_2$ (functional group isomers). The other pairs differ: C$_3$H$_6$O vs C$_4$H$_8$O; C$_5$H$_{12}$ vs C$_5$H$_{10}$; C$_4$H$_8$O vs C$_4$H$_{10}$O.

questions.question:
Iron(III) ions react with thiocyanate ions to form the complex ion $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}$ (equation 1). With excess thiocyanate, $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}$ reacts further to form $\text{Fe(SCN)}_2^{\ +}$ (equation 2).

1. $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 890$
2. $\text{Fe(SCN)}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe(SCN)}_2^{\ +}(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 2.6$

Calculate the $K_{eq}$ for the reaction
$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + 2\text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{Fe(SCN)}_2^{\ +}(aq)$$
questions.answer:
The overall reaction is equation 1 + equation 2, so the equilibrium constants multiply:
$K = 890 \times 2.6 = 2314 \approx 2.3 \times 10^{3}$.

questions.question:
Consider the system:
$$\text{HF}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{F}^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$
Which of the following represents a conjugate acid–base pair present in this system?
questions.answer: A conjugate pair differs by one proton. HF donates H$^+$ to become F$^-$, so HF/F$^-$ is a conjugate acid–base pair (the other pair is H$_3$O$^+$/H$_2$O).

questions.question: Which of the following fragments could give rise to an ion peak in the mass spectrum of 1-chloro-2-methylpropane?
questions.answer: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$. Breaking the C–Cl bond gives the fragment $[\text{C}_4\text{H}_9]^+$ ($m/z = 57$). CH$_4$ and CH$_3$Cl cannot be formed by simply breaking bonds in the molecule (no carbon has 4 H, and the Cl-carbon is a CH$_2$), and C$_3$H$_9$ is not a possible fragment (too many H for 3 C).

questions.question:
| Indicator | Colour & pH | Colour & pH |
|---|---|---|
| Phenol red | Yellow $\le 6.8$ | Red $\ge 8.4$ |
| Methyl orange | Red $\le 3.1$ | Yellow $\ge 4.4$ |

A small quantity of soil was added to 5 mL of pure water, stirred for 5 minutes, allowed to settle and filtered. When one sample of the filtrate was tested with phenol red, the colour turned yellow. When another sample was tested with methyl orange, the colour turned yellow.

What is the best conclusion about the soil?
options: That it is slightly acidic and has a pH less than 8.4.
That it is slightly acidic and has a pH less than 6.8.
That it is slightly alkaline and has a pH less than 6.8.
That it is very acidic and has a pH less than 4.4.
questions.answer: Phenol red yellow means pH $\le 6.8$; methyl orange yellow means pH $\ge 4.4$. So $4.4 \le \text{pH} \le 6.8$: the soil is slightly acidic with a pH less than 6.8.

questions.question:
An experiment to test buffers was carried out in class. The screenshot shows the pH curves (labelled 1–4) obtained when buffered and unbuffered solutions were tested by adding drops of acid or base.

Identify the correct label for each of the graphs.

| | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | buffered solution with base added | unbuffered solution with base added | unbuffered solution with acid added | buffered solution with acid added |
| **B** | unbuffered solution with base added | buffered solution with base added | buffered solution with acid added | unbuffered solution with acid added |
| **C** | unbuffered solution with base added | buffered solution with acid added | buffered solution with base added | unbuffered solution with acid added |
| **D** | buffered solution with acid added | unbuffered solution with acid added | unbuffered solution with base added | buffered solution with base added |
questions.answer: A buffer resists change in pH, so the two nearly flat curves (2 and 3) are buffered. Curve 1 rises sharply (unbuffered + base); curve 2 rises very slightly (buffered + base); curve 3 falls slightly (buffered + acid); curve 4 falls sharply (unbuffered + acid).

questions.question: Which sequence of reagents would be most suitable to convert 1-chloro-2-methylpropane to 2-methylpropene?
options: Water with an acid catalyst, then hydrogen with a platinum catalyst
Acidified MnO$_4^-$, then water with an acid catalyst
questions.answer: NaOH$(aq)$ substitutes OH for Cl: $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH} + \text{Cl}^-$ (2-methylpropan-1-ol). Heating with concentrated H$_2$SO$_4$ then dehydrates the alcohol to 2-methylpropene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}{=}\text{CH}_2$.

questions.question:
At a certain temperature, the equilibrium constant, $K$, for the following reaction is 75.
$$2\text{O}_3(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{O}_2(g)$$
0.3 mol of O$_3$ and 1.5 mol of O$_2$ were introduced into a 5 L reaction vessel. Which is the direction of the equilibrium shift and the reason for the shift?

| | Direction favoured | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| A | Left | $Q > K$ |
| B | Left | $Q < K$ |
| C | Right | $Q > K$ |
| D | Right | $Q < K$ |
questions.answer:
$[\text{O}_3] = 0.3/5 = 0.06$ M, $[\text{O}_2] = 1.5/5 = 0.30$ M.
$Q = \dfrac{[\text{O}_2]^3}{[\text{O}_3]^2} = \dfrac{0.30^3}{0.06^2} = \dfrac{0.027}{0.0036} = 7.5$.
Since $Q < K$ (7.5 < 75), the forward reaction is favoured: shift to the right.

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium process:
$$\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -136\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Which of the following changes would increase the rate of the forward reaction AND cause the equilibrium to shift in the forward direction?
options: The concentration of H$_2$ in the equilibrium mixture is increased
The concentration of CH$_3$CH$_3$ in the equilibrium mixture is increased
questions.answer: Adding H$_2$ increases the frequency of collisions between reactant molecules, so the forward rate increases, and by Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium shifts right to use up the added H$_2$. Decreasing temperature shifts right but slows the forward rate; decreasing pressure shifts left; adding ethane shifts left.

questions.question: The concentrations of species in an equilibrium reaction are shown in the graph. A reaction that matches the changes shown in the graph is:
questions.answer: Two species decrease (reactants) and one increases from zero (product). The blue reactant falls by about the same amount as the product rises, while the purple reactant falls by about half that amount, so the mole ratio is 2 : 1 : 2. This matches $2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3$.

questions.question:
Deuterium (symbol D) is an isotope of hydrogen. Water made from deuterium has the symbol D$_2$O and has similar properties to normal water. D$_2$O ionises according to the equilibrium:
$$\text{D}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{D}^+(aq) + \text{OD}^-(aq) \qquad K_{eq} = 1.82 \times 10^{-16} \text{ at } 25\ ^{\circ}\text{C}$$
In a neutral solution of pure D$_2$O at 25 °C, [D$^+$], in mol L$^{-1}$, is:
questions.answer: D$_2$O is a pure liquid, so $K_{eq} = [\text{D}^+][\text{OD}^-]$. In a neutral solution $[\text{D}^+] = [\text{OD}^-]$, so $[\text{D}^+] = \sqrt{1.82 \times 10^{-16}} = 1.35 \times 10^{-8}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
A saturated solution of magnesium sulfate was placed in a beaker. Solid magnesium sulfate containing radioactive sulfur-35 was added to the solution. The beaker was left overnight and then the mixture was filtered.

Radioactive sulfur-35 would be expected to be found in which of the following?
options: Neither the residue nor the filtrate
questions.answer: A saturated solution in contact with undissolved solid is in dynamic equilibrium: $\text{MgSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{\,2-}(aq)$. Labelled sulfate ions continually dissolve while other ions precipitate at the same rate, so S-35 ends up in both the solid residue and the filtrate.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements best describes the primary differences between the Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry acid theories?

i. The Arrhenius theory defines acids as proton donors, while the Brønsted–Lowry theory defines acids as proton acceptors.
ii. The Arrhenius theory defines acids as substances that contain hydrogen and increase the concentration of hydrogen ions (H$^+$) in aqueous solutions, while the Brønsted–Lowry theory defines acids as proton donors.
iii. The Arrhenius theory applies only to reactions in aqueous solutions, while the Brønsted–Lowry theory applies to reactions in both aqueous and non-aqueous solutions.
iv. The Arrhenius theory defines acids and bases in terms of electron pair acceptors and donors, while the Brønsted–Lowry theory defines them in terms of proton donors and acceptors.
questions.answer: Statements ii and iii are correct. Statement i is wrong (Brønsted–Lowry acids are proton donors) and statement iv describes the Lewis theory, not Arrhenius.

questions.question:
The diagram shows equilibrium mixtures of A$_2$, B$_2$ and AB at two different temperatures, where $T_2 > T_1$.

Which of the following is true for the reaction $\text{A}_2 + \text{B}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{AB}$?
options: It is neither exothermic or endothermic
There is not enough information to determine whether it is exothermic or endothermic.
questions.answer: At $T_1$ there are 5 AB, 1 A$_2$ and 2 B$_2$ molecules; at the higher temperature $T_2$ there are only 3 AB, 2 A$_2$ and 3 B$_2$. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the left (reactants), so the reverse reaction is endothermic and the forward reaction is exothermic.

questions.question: The shapes around the numbered atoms (C1, C2, C3) in the molecule shown are best described by which of the following options?
options: C1 linear, C2 trigonal planar, C3 tetrahedral
C1 tetrahedral, C2 trigonal planar, C3 linear
C1 trigonal planar, C2 linear, C3 tetrahedral
C1 tetrahedral, C2 linear, C3 trigonal planar
questions.answer: C1 has four single bonds (tetrahedral); C2 is part of a C=C double bond (three electron domains, trigonal planar); C3 is part of a C≡C triple bond (two domains, linear).

questions.question:
A student prepared an indicator from red cabbage by boiling red cabbage leaves in water for twenty minutes. They recorded the colour of the indicator at pH intervals of 2:

| pH | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Colour | red | pink | violet | blue | blue-green | green | yellow-green |

The student used the indicator to test four solutions of unknown concentration: HCl – pink; CH$_3$COOH – pink; NaHCO$_3$ – blue; NaOH – blue-green.

Which of the following conclusions is consistent with the observed results?
options: The concentrations of the HCl and the NaOH were both 0.0001 M.
The concentrations of the HCl and CH$_3$COOH were both 0.01 M.
The concentrations of the NaOH and NaHCO$_3$ were both 0.01 M.
The concentrations of the HCl and NaHCO$_3$ were both 0.01 M.
questions.answer: HCl pink → pH ≈ 4 → $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-4}$ M, so 0.0001 M strong acid. NaOH blue-green → pH ≈ 10 → pOH = 4 → $[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-4}$ M, so 0.0001 M strong base. 0.01 M HCl would be pH 2 (red) and 0.01 M NaOH pH 12 (green), ruling out B, C and D.

questions.question: The $^{13}$C NMR spectrum of an organic compound is shown. The organic compound could be:
questions.answer: The spectrum has 5 peaks (5 carbon environments): two in the alkene region (≈138 and ≈115 ppm), one at ≈62 ppm (C–OH) and two at ≈30–35 ppm. Only B and D contain C=C; a terminal =CH$_2$ appears near 115 ppm and the =CH– near 138 ppm, matching pent-4-en-1-ol (D). In B (pent-3-en-1-ol) both alkene carbons would appear close together at about 125–135 ppm. A and C have no peaks above 100 ppm.

questions.question:
(i) Draw the structural formula of 2-chloro-3-methylpentanoic acid.

(ii) Draw the structural formula of 3-ethylhexan-2-amine.

(iii) Give the IUPAC name of the compound shown.
questions.answer:
(i) 2-chloro-3-methylpentanoic acid: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CHClCOOH}$ — a 5-carbon chain with the COOH carbon as C1, Cl on C2 and a CH$_3$ branch on C3 (all H shown in a full structural formula).

(ii) 3-ethylhexan-2-amine: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(NH}_2)\text{CH(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ — a 6-carbon chain with NH$_2$ on C2 and an ethyl branch on C3.

(iii) The ester is formed from propanoic acid (the 3-carbon C=O side) and butan-1-ol (the 4-carbon O-alkyl side): **butyl propanoate**.

questions.question:
Formic acid, a weak acid, has the formula HCOOH and its p$K_a$ is 3.75.

Calculate the pH of a 0.25 M solution of formic acid at 25 °C.
questions.answer:
$\text{HCOOH}(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCOO}^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq)$

$K_a = 10^{-\text{p}K_a} = 10^{-3.75} = 1.778 \times 10^{-4}$

$K_a = \dfrac{[\text{HCOO}^-][\text{H}^+]}{[\text{HCOOH}]}$. Let $[\text{H}^+] = [\text{HCOO}^-] = x$; since the acid is weak, $x \ll 0.25$ so $[\text{HCOOH}] \approx 0.25$ M.

$x^2 = 1.778 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.25 = 4.446 \times 10^{-5}$, so $x = 6.67 \times 10^{-3}$ M

$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(6.67 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.18$

questions.question: Formic acid (HCOOH) can react with potassium hydroxide to produce a salt and water. Write an equation for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$$\text{HCOOH}(aq) + \text{KOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{HCOOK}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(the salt is potassium methanoate/formate, $\text{KHCOO}$).

questions.question: Formic acid (HCOOH, a weak acid) reacts with potassium hydroxide to form the salt potassium formate (KHCOO) and water. State whether you would expect this salt to be acidic, neutral or basic. Explain your answer including an appropriate chemical equation.
questions.answer:
The salt is **basic**.

The formate ion, HCOO$^-$, is the conjugate base of the weak acid formic acid, so it is a relatively strong conjugate base and accepts protons from water:
$$\text{HCOO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCOOH}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$$
This produces OH$^-$ ions, so $[\text{OH}^-] > [\text{H}^+]$ and pH > 7. The K$^+$ ion comes from the strong base KOH, is a negligibly weak conjugate acid and does not react with water, so it does not affect the pH.

questions.question:
50.0 mL of a solution of HCl with a pH of 3.0 was mixed with 30.0 mL of a solution of HNO$_3$ with a pH of 5.0.

Calculate the pH of the resultant solution.

Ethanoic acid and ethanamide have similar molar masses but significantly different boiling points:

| | Ethanoic acid | Ethanamide |
|---|---|---|
| MM (g mol$^{-1}$) | 60 | 59 |
| Boiling point (°C) | 118 | 222 |

Explain the difference in the boiling points of these two compounds. Include a diagram in your response.
questions.answer:
**Diagram:** draw two ethanoic acid molecules ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) side by side with a dotted hydrogen bond from the H of one O–H group to the C=O oxygen of the other (they commonly form a dimer joined by two hydrogen bonds). Then draw several ethanamide molecules ($\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$), with dotted hydrogen bonds from **each** of the two N–H hydrogens to the C=O oxygen (or N) of neighbouring molecules, forming an extended network.

**Explanation:** Both molecules have similar molar masses and so have similar dispersion forces, and both are polar (dipole–dipole forces). Both can also hydrogen bond, through the carbonyl O and the O–H (acid) or N–H (amide) groups. However, the –NH$_2$ group of ethanamide has **two** H atoms bonded to the electronegative N, whereas ethanoic acid has only **one** H on its hydroxyl group. Each ethanamide molecule can therefore form more hydrogen bonds with its neighbours, giving a more extensive network of strong intermolecular forces. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ethanamide has the much higher boiling point (222 °C compared with 118 °C).

questions.question: Ibuprofen, $\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{17}\text{COOH}$, is a monoprotic acid. Write a balanced chemical equation for the reaction between ibuprofen and sodium hydroxide.
questions.answer: $$\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{17}\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{17}\text{COONa}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

questions.question:
A chemist needed to check the composition of Nurofen tablets, which contain the active ingredient ibuprofen ($\text{C}_{12}\text{H}_{17}\text{COOH}$, $M = 206.27$ g mol$^{-1}$), a monoprotic acid.

A Nurofen tablet with a mass of 256 mg was crushed to a fine powder, dissolved in water and transferred to a 125.0 mL volumetric flask, adding water accurately up to the mark. Four 25.0 mL aliquots of this solution were then titrated against a 0.00502 M standard solution of sodium hydroxide to a phenolphthalein end point.

| Titration run | Titre (mL) |
|---|---|
| 1 | 39.65 |
| 2 | 38.60 |
| 3 | 38.55 |
| 4 | 38.65 |

Determine the percentage composition by mass of ibuprofen in the Nurofen tablet.
questions.answer:
Run 1 is a rough titre (not concordant) and is excluded.

Average titre $= \dfrac{38.60 + 38.55 + 38.65}{3} = 38.60$ mL

$n(\text{NaOH}) = cV = 0.00502 \times 0.03860 = 1.938 \times 10^{-4}$ mol

Ibuprofen : NaOH = 1 : 1, so $n(\text{ibuprofen})$ in 25.0 mL $= 1.938 \times 10^{-4}$ mol

In 125.0 mL: $n = 1.938 \times 10^{-4} \times \dfrac{125.0}{25.0} = 9.689 \times 10^{-4}$ mol

$m = nM = 9.689 \times 10^{-4} \times 206.27 = 0.1999$ g $= 199.9$ mg

$\%\ \text{ibuprofen} = \dfrac{199.9}{256} \times 100 = 78.1\%$

questions.question:
Ammonia is manufactured industrially by the Haber process:
$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Write the equilibrium constant expression for this reaction.

Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process:
$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Some hydrogen, nitrogen and ammonia were sealed in a reaction vessel and the forward and reverse reaction rates were monitored over time, as shown in the graph.

A change was made to the system at 5 minutes. Identify this change and use collision theory to explain the shapes of the curves between 5 and 8 minutes.
questions.answer:
**Change:** some reactant (N$_2$ and/or H$_2$) was removed, decreasing the concentration of reactants. At 5 minutes the forward rate drops suddenly while the reverse rate is initially unchanged, so only the reactant concentration changed.

**Explanation:** With fewer reactant molecules per unit volume, there are fewer collisions between N$_2$ and H$_2$ molecules per second, so the forward rate falls immediately. The reverse rate is now greater than the forward rate, so the reverse reaction is favoured. As NH$_3$ decomposes, [NH$_3$] decreases, so the frequency of collisions between NH$_3$ molecules falls and the reverse rate gradually decreases. At the same time N$_2$ and H$_2$ are produced, so their concentrations rise, collisions between them become more frequent and the forward rate gradually increases. By about 6–8 minutes the forward and reverse rates are equal again and a new equilibrium is established (at lower rates than before).

questions.question:
Ammonia is manufactured by the Haber process:
$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
The graph shows the forward and reverse reaction rates in a sealed vessel over time.

At 9 minutes, a temperature OR pressure change was applied to the system. With reference to the graph and Le Chatelier's principle, justify which change was applied to the system at this time.
questions.answer:
The change was an **increase in temperature**.

At 9 minutes both the forward and reverse rates increase suddenly, but the reverse rate increases more than the forward rate. An increase in temperature increases the rates of both reactions, but increases the rate of the endothermic reaction (here the reverse reaction, since the forward reaction is exothermic) by more. Le Chatelier's principle predicts that when temperature is increased the system shifts to minimise the change by favouring the endothermic (reverse) reaction, which is what the graph shows. As NH$_3$ is used up the reverse rate then falls, and as N$_2$ and H$_2$ form the forward rate rises, until the rates are equal at a new equilibrium.

An increase in pressure (decrease in volume) would instead favour the forward reaction (4 mol of gas → 2 mol), so the forward rate would have increased more than the reverse rate; this is not what is observed.

questions.question:
Methyl butanoate is an ester that is a component of pineapple flavouring.

Draw the structural formula equation for the formation of methyl butanoate from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid. Include all relevant reaction conditions.
questions.answer:
Methanol + butanoic acid ⇌ methyl butanoate + water, catalysed by concentrated sulfuric acid and heated under reflux:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} \;\underset{\text{heat (reflux)}}{\overset{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4}{\rightleftharpoons}}\; \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
In the structural formula equation, draw all bonds: H$_3$C–O–H + HO–C(=O)–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_3$ → H$_3$C–O–C(=O)–CH$_2$–CH$_2$–CH$_3$ + H–O–H, with all C–H bonds shown.

questions.question: Methyl butanoate is prepared from methanol and butanoic acid. Justify the need to reflux the reaction mixture to produce the ester product.
questions.answer: Esterification is very slow at room temperature, so the mixture must be heated to increase the reaction rate (and to allow the reversible reaction to approach equilibrium in a reasonable time). However, the reactants (especially methanol) and the ester product are volatile and would evaporate and be lost if heated in an open vessel. Refluxing uses a vertical (Liebig) condenser so that vapours condense and drip back into the reaction flask. This allows prolonged heating without loss of reactants or product, which increases the yield of ester, and it also stops flammable organic vapours escaping into the laboratory, where they could be ignited.

questions.question:
A chemist prepared methyl butanoate by combining 3.50 g of methanol with 5.75 g of butanoic acid. The mass of the product was found to be only 24% of the expected result.

What was the mass of the product extracted?
questions.answer:
$\text{CH}_3\text{OH} + \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOCH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (1 : 1 : 1)

$n(\text{CH}_3\text{OH}) = \dfrac{3.50}{32.042} = 0.1092$ mol

$n(\text{C}_3\text{H}_7\text{COOH}) = \dfrac{5.75}{88.104} = 0.06526$ mol → butanoic acid is the limiting reagent.

Theoretical $n(\text{ester}) = 0.06526$ mol; $M(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2) = 102.13$ g mol$^{-1}$

Theoretical mass $= 0.06526 \times 102.13 = 6.665$ g

Actual mass $= 0.24 \times 6.665 = 1.60$ g

questions.question:
Ionic compounds can form saturated solutions in water.

Explain the processes involved when an ionic compound dissolves in water. Use diagrams to support your explanation.
questions.answer:
**Diagram:** a cation (e.g. Na$^+$) surrounded by water molecules with their partially negative O atoms pointing towards it, and an anion (e.g. Cl$^-$) surrounded by water molecules with their partially positive H atoms pointing towards it (ion–dipole attractions).

**Explanation:** Water is a polar molecule. When an ionic solid is placed in water, the $\delta^-$ oxygen atoms of water are attracted to the cations and the $\delta^+$ hydrogen atoms are attracted to the anions at the surface of the lattice (ion–dipole forces). Energy is required to break the ionic bonds in the lattice (lattice energy) and to separate water molecules, while energy is released when the separated ions become surrounded by water molecules (hydration/solvation). The ions are pulled from the lattice and dispersed through the solution as hydrated ions, e.g. $\text{NaCl}(s) \rightarrow \text{Na}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)$. The compound dissolves readily when the energy released on hydration is comparable to or greater than the energy needed to break the lattice. In a saturated solution, dissolution and precipitation occur at equal rates (dynamic equilibrium).

questions.question: Lead(II) sulfate is an ionic compound used in lead–acid batteries. Write the equilibrium expression, $K_{sp}$, for a saturated solution of lead(II) sulfate.
questions.answer:
$\text{PbSO}_4(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Pb}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{\,2-}(aq)$
$$K_{sp} = [\text{Pb}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{\,2-}]$$

questions.question: Calculate the solubility of lead(II) sulfate at 25 °C, in grams per 100 mL. ($K_{sp}(\text{PbSO}_4) = 2.53 \times 10^{-8}$ at 25 °C.)

An alkene, C$_5$H$_{10}$, reacts with HBr to give two products, A and B. A reacts with NaOH to give C, and B reacts with NaOH to give D. When C is heated with acidified permanganate (H$^+$/MnO$_4^-$) there is no reaction. When D is heated with acidified permanganate it forms E, and E produces no bubbles when Na$_2$CO$_3$ is added (see the flow chart).

Draw the structural formula and name each of the molecules A to E.
questions.answer:
C is not oxidised, so it is a **tertiary** alcohol; D is oxidised to E, which does not react with carbonate (not a carboxylic acid), so D is a **secondary** alcohol and E is a ketone. Both bromoalkanes come from HBr adding across the same C=C bond, so the alkene must be 2-methylbut-2-ene, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}{=}\text{CHCH}_3$.

- **A**: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$
- **B**: 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCHBrCH}_3$
- **C**: 2-methylbutan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (tertiary – not oxidised)
- **D**: 3-methylbutan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH(OH)CH}_3$ (secondary)
- **E**: 3-methylbutan-2-one, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOCH}_3$ (ketone – no CO$_2$ with Na$_2$CO$_3$)

Each should be drawn as a full structural formula showing all bonds.

questions.question:
A group of students used the polystyrene-cup calorimeter shown to determine the heat of neutralisation for an acid/base reaction. They added 200.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid (HNO$_3$) to 200.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ potassium hydroxide (KOH) and stirred the mixture. An initial temperature of 22.7 °C and a final temperature of 26.4 °C were recorded.

Calculate the molar enthalpy of neutralisation between nitric acid and potassium hydroxide. (Take the specific heat capacity of the solution as $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$ and its density as 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$.)
questions.answer:
$\text{HNO}_3(aq) + \text{KOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{KNO}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = n(\text{HNO}_3) = cV = 1.00 \times 0.2000 = 0.200$ mol

Mass of solution $= 400.0$ g $= 0.4000$ kg, $\Delta T = 26.4 - 22.7 = 3.7$ K

$q = mc\Delta T = 0.4000 \times 4.18 \times 10^{3} \times 3.7 = 6186$ J $= 6.19$ kJ

$\Delta H = -\dfrac{q}{n} = -\dfrac{6.19}{0.200} = -30.9$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ (exothermic)

questions.question:
Students mixed 200.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ HNO$_3$ with 200.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ KOH in a polystyrene-cup calorimeter and calculated a molar enthalpy of neutralisation of about $-31$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. The theoretical enthalpy of neutralisation of any strong acid and strong base is $-57$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Explain the effect of ONE source of error on the calculated enthalpy of neutralisation.
questions.answer: Heat is lost from the reaction mixture to the surroundings (through the cup walls, the gap around the thermometer in the lid, and by heating the cup and thermometer themselves). As a result the measured temperature rise $\Delta T$ is smaller than it should be. Since $q = mc\Delta T$, the calculated heat released $q$ is also smaller than the true value, and because $\Delta H = -q/n$, the magnitude of the calculated enthalpy of neutralisation is smaller (less negative) than the theoretical $-57$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, as seen in the result of about $-31$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Describe an application of neutralisation reactions in everyday life. Include a balanced chemical equation in your answer.
questions.answer:
Antacids are used to relieve heartburn and indigestion, which are caused by excess hydrochloric acid in the stomach. An antacid containing a weak base such as magnesium hydroxide is swallowed and neutralises the excess stomach acid, raising the pH and relieving the discomfort:
$$\text{Mg(OH)}_2(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
(Other acceptable examples: liming acidic soils with CaCO$_3$ or Ca(OH)$_2$; treating bee stings with baking soda; neutralising acid spills with NaHCO$_3$.)

questions.question: Determine whether a precipitate will form when 50.0 mL of 0.052 M Ba(OH)$_2$ is mixed with 50.0 mL of 0.049 M Na$_2$SO$_4$. ($K_{sp}(\text{BaSO}_4) = 1.08 \times 10^{-10}$.)
questions.answer:
Possible precipitate: $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{\,2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$ (NaOH is soluble).

After mixing, the total volume is 100.0 mL, so each solution is diluted by a factor of 2 ($c_1V_1 = c_2V_2$):

$[\text{Ba}^{2+}] = \dfrac{0.052 \times 50.0}{100.0} = 0.026$ M, $\quad [\text{SO}_4^{\,2-}] = \dfrac{0.049 \times 50.0}{100.0} = 0.0245$ M

$Q = [\text{Ba}^{2+}][\text{SO}_4^{\,2-}] = 0.026 \times 0.0245 = 6.4 \times 10^{-4}$

Since $Q = 6.4 \times 10^{-4} > K_{sp} = 1.08 \times 10^{-10}$, a precipitate of BaSO$_4$ **will form**.

questions.question:
A range of analysis techniques were performed on a sample of a substance found in wine. Percentage composition analysis revealed C: 62.0%, H: 10.4%, O: 27.6%. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR spectrum and $^1$H NMR spectrum are shown (in that order), with the following $^1$H NMR data:

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 6 | doublet |
| 1.2 | 3 | triplet |
| 2.6 | 1 | septet |
| 4.2 | 2 | quartet |

With reference to the percentage composition and the mass spectrum, determine the molecular formula of the compound.
questions.answer:
Mole ratio C : H : O $= \dfrac{62.0}{12.01} : \dfrac{10.4}{1.008} : \dfrac{27.6}{16.00} = 5.16 : 10.3 : 1.725 = 3 : 6 : 1$

Empirical formula C$_3$H$_6$O, with $M = 58$ g mol$^{-1}$. The molecular ion peak in the mass spectrum is at $m/z = 116 = 2 \times 58$, so the molecular formula is **C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_2$**.

questions.question:
A range of analysis techniques were performed on a sample of a substance found in wine. Percentage composition analysis revealed C: 62.0%, H: 10.4%, O: 27.6%. The infrared spectrum, mass spectrum, $^{13}$C NMR spectrum and $^1$H NMR spectrum are shown (in that order), with the following $^1$H NMR data:

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 1.1 | 6 | doublet |
| 1.2 | 3 | triplet |
| 2.6 | 1 | septet |
| 4.2 | 2 | quartet |

The molecular formula of the compound is C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_2$. Draw the structural formula of the compound and justify your decision by referring to data in all the spectra provided.
questions.answer:
The compound is **ethyl 2-methylpropanoate**, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH–COO–CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (draw with all bonds: two CH$_3$ groups on a CH, bonded to C(=O)–O–CH$_2$–CH$_3$).

**IR:** strong, sharp absorption at about 1740 cm$^{-1}$ = C=O; strong absorption near 1200–1250 cm$^{-1}$ = C–O; no broad O–H absorption at 2500–3300 cm$^{-1}$ or 3200–3600 cm$^{-1}$, so it is not an acid or alcohol. C–H at about 2900–3000 cm$^{-1}$. With two O atoms and one C=O, it is an ester.

**Mass spectrum:** M$^+$ at $m/z = 116$ (C$_6$H$_{12}$O$_2$). $m/z = 71$ = $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCO}]^+$ (loss of OCH$_2$CH$_3$); base peak $m/z = 43$ = $[(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}]^+$; $m/z = 29$ = $[\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2]^+$.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** 5 peaks for 6 carbons, so two carbons are equivalent (the two CH$_3$ groups of the isopropyl group). ≈177 ppm: ester C=O; ≈60 ppm: CH$_2$ bonded to O; ≈34 ppm: CH next to C=O; ≈19 ppm (tallest): the two equivalent CH$_3$ on the CH; ≈14 ppm: CH$_3$ of the ethyl group.

**$^1$H NMR:** 4 proton environments (6 : 3 : 1 : 2 = 12 H).
- 4.2 ppm, 2H, quartet: –O–CH$_2$– (shifted downfield by the O), next to a CH$_3$ (3 neighbours → quartet).
- 1.2 ppm, 3H, triplet: CH$_3$ of the ethyl group, next to CH$_2$ (2 neighbours → triplet).
- 2.6 ppm, 1H, septet: –CH– next to C=O, with 6 neighbouring H (two CH$_3$) → septet.
- 1.1 ppm, 6H, doublet: two equivalent CH$_3$ groups each next to the single CH → doublet.

The ethyl group is on the O side (CH$_2$ at 4.2 ppm, 3.5–5.0 ppm range for esters) and the isopropyl group is on the C=O side (CH at 2.6 ppm), confirming ethyl 2-methylpropanoate rather than isopropyl propanoate.

questions.question:
The labels for five organic compounds in a laboratory store cupboard have been lost. The compounds are known to be pentane, pentan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol, pentan-3-one and pentanoic acid.

**Clues**
1. The $^{13}$C NMR spectrum of B has three peaks.
2. The $^{13}$C NMR spectrum of C has three peaks.
3. A forms D by reaction with acidified MnO$_4^-$.
4. E forms B by reaction with acidified MnO$_4^-$.

| Compound | A | B | C | D | E |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Boiling point (°C) | 138 | 102 | 36.1 | 186 | 116 |

Use the clues and the boiling point data to identify the five compounds. Draw the structural formula of each compound and justify your identifications with reference to specific data, structural formulae and/or relevant chemical equations.
questions.answer:
**A = pentan-1-ol** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$; **B = pentan-3-one** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$; **C = pentane** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$; **D = pentanoic acid** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$; **E = pentan-3-ol** $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (each drawn as a full structural formula).

**Justification**
- Only the symmetrical molecules pentane, pentan-3-ol and pentan-3-one have three carbon environments, so B and C are two of these (clues 1, 2).
- E is oxidised by acidified permanganate to B (clue 4). A secondary alcohol is oxidised to a ketone, so E is pentan-3-ol and B is pentan-3-one: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Therefore C, the remaining symmetrical compound, is pentane.
- A is oxidised to D (clue 3): a primary alcohol is oxidised to a carboxylic acid, so A is pentan-1-ol and D is pentanoic acid: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+/\text{MnO}_4^-} \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{COOH}$.

**Boiling points confirm this:** all five have similar dispersion forces (5 carbons).
