| I | $4.0 \times 10^{-4}$ | $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ | 0 |
| C | $-1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ | $-4 \times 1.8 \times 10^{-4} = -7.2 \times 10^{-4}$ | $+1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| E | $2.2 \times 10^{-4}$ | $7.8 \times 10^{-4}$ | $1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ |

Total volume $= 6.00$ mL $= 0.00600$ L, so at equilibrium:
$[\text{Cu}^{2+}] = 0.0367$, $[\text{NH}_3] = 0.130$, $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4^{2+}] = 0.0300$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4^{2+}]}{[\text{Cu}^{2+}][\text{NH}_3]^4} = \frac{0.0300}{0.0367 \times (0.130)^4} \approx 2.9 \times 10^{3}$$

(Common errors: forgetting that the total volume is 6 mL, or using moles instead of mol L$^{-1}$ in $K_{eq}$.)

questions.question:
A student investigated the heat released during the neutralisation of sulfuric acid with sodium hydroxide in the following experiment.

25.0 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH was mixed with 15.0 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ in an insulated container. Both solutions were initially at 21.0 °C, and the final temperature of the mixture was 24.5 °C.

The solutions are assumed to have a density of 1.00 g mL$^{-1}$ and a specific heat capacity of $4.18 \times 10^{3}$ J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.

Calculate the experimental molar heat of neutralisation.
questions.answer:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.50 \times 0.0250 = 0.0125$ mol; $n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4) = 0.50 \times 0.0150 = 0.0075$ mol, which needs $0.015$ mol NaOH — so NaOH is limiting and $n(\text{H}_2\text{O formed}) = 0.0125$ mol.

Mass of solution $= 25.0 + 15.0 = 40.0$ mL → $40.0$ g $= 0.0400$ kg; $\Delta T = 24.5 - 21.0 = 3.5$ K.

$q = mc\Delta T = 0.0400 \times 4.18 \times 10^3 \times 3.5 = 585.2$ J

$$\Delta H = -\frac{q}{n(\text{H}_2\text{O})} = -\frac{0.5852\ \text{kJ}}{0.0125\ \text{mol}} = -46.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

(The enthalpy of neutralisation is per mole of water formed.)

questions.question:
A student mixed 25.0 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH with 15.0 mL of 0.50 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ in an insulated container and calculated an experimental molar heat of neutralisation of $-46.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

The accepted molar heat of neutralisation is $-57.3$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.

Compare the difference between the experimental and accepted values and provide a reason for the difference between these two values.
questions.answer:
The magnitude of the experimental value (46.8 kJ mol$^{-1}$) is lower than the accepted value (57.3 kJ mol$^{-1}$) by about 10.5 kJ mol$^{-1}$, i.e. about 18% less heat was measured than expected.

This is most likely because some of the heat released was lost to the surroundings (through the container walls, lid and thermometer, and absorbed by the container itself) rather than raising the temperature of the solution, so the measured $\Delta T$, and hence $q$, was too small. (Assuming the solution has the density and specific heat capacity of pure water also introduces some error.)

questions.question:
A student is investigating the buffering capacity of blood. Blood acts as a buffer solution, primarily through the presence of carbonic acid and hydrogen carbonate.

A sample of blood is placed in a beaker and connected to a pH meter. Small amounts of 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl(aq) and 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH(aq) are added separately.

The student observes that the pH changes very little in each case.

Using at least one equation to support your answer, explain the lack of change in pH.
questions.answer:
Blood contains significant amounts of both a weak acid, $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$, and its conjugate base, $\text{HCO}_3^-$, in equilibrium:

$$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$$

- **Adding HCl:** the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ increases its concentration, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (Le Chatelier's principle): $\text{HCO}_3^-$ reacts with the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to form $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$. Most of the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ is consumed, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ and the pH change very little.
- **Adding NaOH:** the $\text{OH}^-$ reacts with $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ (or directly with $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$: $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3 + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$). The decrease in $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ causes the equilibrium to shift to the right, with $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ ionising to replace most of the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ removed, so the pH rises only slightly.

Because large reservoirs of both $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and $\text{HCO}_3^-$ are present, small additions of acid or base are absorbed and the pH stays nearly constant.

questions.question:
A mixture of carbon monoxide, chlorine and carbonyl dichloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gases was placed in a closed container. The concentrations of the gases were monitored over time, as shown in the graph. (From 0 to 2 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ falls from about 0.46 to 0.40 and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ from about 0.37 to 0.30 mol L$^{-1}$, while $[\text{COCl}_2]$ rises from about 0.13 to 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$; all are constant from 2 to 4 minutes; after 4 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ rise gradually and $[\text{COCl}_2]$ falls gradually until all become constant again at about 7 minutes, at about 0.52, 0.42 and 0.085 mol L$^{-1}$.)

Write the chemical equation for this equilibrium.
questions.answer:
$$\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$$

(From 0–2 min, CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ decrease by the same amount (≈0.07 mol L$^{-1}$) as $\text{COCl}_2$ increases, so the mole ratio is 1 : 1 : 1.)

questions.question:
A mixture of carbon monoxide, chlorine and carbonyl dichloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gases was placed in a closed container. The concentrations of the gases were monitored over time, as shown in the graph. (From 0 to 2 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ falls from about 0.46 to 0.40 and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ from about 0.37 to 0.30 mol L$^{-1}$, while $[\text{COCl}_2]$ rises from about 0.13 to 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$; all are constant from 2 to 4 minutes; after 4 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ rise gradually and $[\text{COCl}_2]$ falls gradually until all become constant again at about 7 minutes, at about 0.52, 0.42 and 0.085 mol L$^{-1}$.)

At what time does the system first reach equilibrium? Justify your answer.
questions.answer: At 2 minutes. From this time the concentrations of all three gases stop changing (the lines become horizontal), showing that the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal — the system is in dynamic equilibrium.

questions.question:
A mixture of carbon monoxide, chlorine and carbonyl dichloride ($\text{COCl}_2$) gases was placed in a closed container. The concentrations of the gases were monitored over time, as shown in the graph. (From 0 to 2 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ falls from about 0.46 to 0.40 and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ from about 0.37 to 0.30 mol L$^{-1}$, while $[\text{COCl}_2]$ rises from about 0.13 to 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$; all are constant from 2 to 4 minutes; after 4 minutes $[\text{CO}]$ and $[\text{Cl}_2]$ rise gradually and $[\text{COCl}_2]$ falls gradually until all become constant again at about 7 minutes, at about 0.52, 0.42 and 0.085 mol L$^{-1}$.)

A change was introduced at four minutes. Explain how the change could impact the equilibrium constant for the reaction $\text{CO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{COCl}_2(g)$.
questions.answer:
At 4 minutes none of the concentrations changes suddenly; instead all three change gradually (CO and $\text{Cl}_2$ increase, $\text{COCl}_2$ decreases) between 4 and 7 minutes. A change of concentration (adding/removing a gas) or of volume/pressure would cause an immediate step change in concentration, so the change must have been a **change in temperature**.

Temperature is the only factor that changes the value of $K_{eq}$. The equilibrium shifted to the left (towards the reactants), so $K_{eq}$ **decreased**:

- before: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{0.20}{0.40 \times 0.30} \approx 1.7$
- after: $K_{eq} \approx \dfrac{0.085}{0.52 \times 0.42} \approx 0.39$

If the forward reaction is exothermic (it is — forming $\text{COCl}_2$ releases heat), the temperature was increased, which favours the endothermic reverse reaction and lowers $K_{eq}$. (Had the forward reaction been endothermic, a decrease in temperature would produce the same shift and also lower $K_{eq}$.)

questions.question:
Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy (AAS) was used to determine the concentration of lead in groundwater soil samples.

The absorbances of lead samples of known concentration were also measured:

| Concentration $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ (ppm) | 1.00 | 2.00 | 3.00 | 4.00 | 5.00 | 6.00 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Absorbance | 0.084 | 0.178 | 0.247 | 0.321 | 0.424 | 0.498 |

The absorbance of the analysed groundwater was measured as 0.35. The safe concentration of lead in water is less than 0.0038 g/L.

Graph the calibration curve and determine if the lead levels in the groundwater are safe.
questions.answer:
**Calibration curve (4 marks):** plot absorbance (y-axis, labelled, 0–0.6) against concentration of $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ in ppm (x-axis, labelled, 0–7), with an even scale on each axis, plot the six points accurately and draw a straight line of best fit (gradient ≈ 0.082 ppm$^{-1}$, passing very close to the origin).

**Determination (2 marks):** reading across from absorbance 0.35 to the line and down gives
$$[\text{Pb}^{2+}] \approx 4.2\ \text{ppm} = 4.2\ \text{mg L}^{-1} = \frac{4.2}{1000} = 0.0042\ \text{g L}^{-1}$$

Since $0.0042\ \text{g L}^{-1} > 0.0038\ \text{g L}^{-1}$, the lead level is above the safe limit — the groundwater is **unsafe**.

(A judgement without supporting calculation earned no marks for this part.)

questions.question:
The following table shows the $\text{p}K_a$ of three unknown acids.

| Acid | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{p}K_a$ | 4.76 | 3.8 | 2.6 |

Show how $\text{p}K_a$ relates to acid strength and identify which acid is the strongest.
questions.answer:
Acid strength is the extent to which an acid ionises in water: $\text{HA} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{A}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, with
$$K_a = \frac{[\text{A}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{HA}]}$$
A larger $K_a$ means a greater degree of ionisation, i.e. a stronger acid.

$\text{p}K_a = -\log_{10} K_a$, so a **smaller** $\text{p}K_a$ corresponds to a **larger** $K_a$ and a stronger acid (each unit decrease in $\text{p}K_a$ is a tenfold increase in $K_a$).

Acid C has the lowest $\text{p}K_a$ (2.6, $K_a \approx 2.5 \times 10^{-3}$), so **Acid C is the strongest** of the three.

questions.question:
A student investigated the equilibrium between nitrogen dioxide, which has a red-brown colour, and dinitrogen tetroxide, which is colourless.

$$2\text{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$$

They filled a syringe with nitrogen dioxide (Stage 1). Then they pushed the plunger down, reducing the volume of the gas (Stage 2). They made one observation immediately after the plunger was pushed down and another observation a few minutes later.

Describe the observations the student made and explain the outcome with reference to collision theory.
questions.answer:
**Observations:** immediately after the plunger is pushed down the gas becomes a **darker** red-brown; over the next few minutes the colour **fades to a lighter** red-brown (but not colourless, and still somewhat darker than at Stage 1).

**Explanation:**
- Decreasing the volume immediately increases the concentration of $\text{NO}_2$ (same molecules in a smaller space), so the colour darkens.
- Both gases are now at higher concentration, so the frequency of collisions increases for both reactions. The forward reaction ($2\text{NO}_2 \rightarrow \text{N}_2\text{O}_4$) requires two $\text{NO}_2$ molecules to collide, so its rate depends on $[\text{NO}_2]^2$ and increases more than the rate of the reverse reaction.
- With the forward rate greater than the reverse rate, $\text{NO}_2$ is converted into colourless $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ (the side with fewer gas molecules), so the colour fades until the rates are equal again and a new equilibrium is established (consistent with Le Chatelier's principle).

questions.question:
X decomposes in the following equilibrium:

$$3\text{X}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Y}(g) + \text{Z}(g) \qquad K_{eq} = 0.64 \text{ at } 560\ \text{K}$$

A 2.00 L sealed vessel at a temperature of 560 K contains $4.0 \times 10^{-3}$ moles of X, $3.7 \times 10^{-6}$ moles of Y and $3.7 \times 10^{-6}$ moles of Z.

The system is kept at constant volume and temperature. Determine, with the support of calculations, if the pressure of the system will increase or decrease.
questions.answer:
Concentrations:
$[\text{X}] = \dfrac{4.0 \times 10^{-3}}{2.00} = 2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$; $[\text{Y}] = [\text{Z}] = \dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{-6}}{2.00} = 1.85 \times 10^{-6}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$$Q = \frac{[\text{Y}][\text{Z}]}{[\text{X}]^3} = \frac{(1.85 \times 10^{-6})^2}{(2.0 \times 10^{-3})^3} = \frac{3.42 \times 10^{-12}}{8.0 \times 10^{-9}} = 4.3 \times 10^{-4}$$

$Q < K_{eq}$ ($4.3 \times 10^{-4} < 0.64$), so the system is not at equilibrium and the net reaction proceeds forward (to the right) until $Q = K_{eq}$.

The forward reaction converts 3 mol of gas into 2 mol of gas, so the total number of gas molecules decreases. At constant volume and temperature, pressure is proportional to the number of moles of gas, so the **pressure will decrease**.

questions.question:
The Haber process is used to synthesise ammonia from the following reaction:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure (0–400 atm) for temperatures from 350 °C to 550 °C: yield increases with pressure and decreases with temperature (at 400 atm: about 68% at 350 °C, 43% at 450 °C, 23% at 550 °C).

In industrial settings the temperature is typically kept at around 450 °C. Discuss why this temperature is chosen, considering both reaction rate and equilibrium position.
questions.answer:
The forward reaction is exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle a lower temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right and gives a higher equilibrium yield (the graph shows yield falls as temperature rises). However, at low temperature fewer molecules have energy ≥ the activation energy, so the reaction is too slow to be economical.

Higher temperatures increase the reaction rate but shift the equilibrium towards the reactants, lowering the yield. About 450 °C (with an iron catalyst) is a **compromise** temperature that gives an acceptable rate with a reasonable yield of ammonia.

questions.question:
The Haber process is used to synthesise ammonia from the following reaction:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g) \qquad \Delta H = -92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

The graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure (0–400 atm) for temperatures from 350 °C to 550 °C: yield increases with pressure and decreases with temperature (at 400 atm: about 68% at 350 °C, 43% at 450 °C, 23% at 550 °C).

Justify another important condition that must be considered for this reaction.
questions.answer:
**Pressure.** Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia because the product side has fewer moles of gas (2 mol vs 4 mol), so higher pressure increases the yield (as the graph shows); higher pressure also increases the rate because gas concentrations and collision frequency are greater.

However, very high pressures are expensive to generate and maintain and require thick-walled, costly reactors, and they increase the safety risk of leaks or explosions. So a high but moderate pressure (around 150–300 atm in practice) is used as a compromise between yield, rate, cost and safety.

(Other valid answers: use of an iron catalyst to increase the rate without changing the equilibrium position; removing $\text{NH}_3$ by liquefaction to shift the equilibrium right.)

questions.question:
A student spilled 2 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid on the school laboratory floor. It was neutralised by adding solid sodium acetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) in excess.

Sulfuric acid is a strong acid and sodium acetate is weakly basic. Write a balanced chemical equation for this reaction and draw (or describe) a model of the species in the solution at each stage of the neutralisation: before $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ is added; immediately after some $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ is added; and when $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ has been added in excess.
questions.answer:
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + 2\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq)$$

Models will vary, but they should show these species (plus water molecules) at each stage:

| Stage | Species present |
|---|---|
| Before $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ is added | many $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ (or $\text{H}^+$) ions and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ ions |
| Immediately after some $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ is added | fewer $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$; $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ molecules (mostly un-ionised), a few $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$; $\text{Na}^+$; $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ |
| $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ added in excess | no significant $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$; excess $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$; $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$; $\text{Na}^+$; $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ |

The salts formed ($\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) are soluble, so they are shown as separate aqueous ions, not as solids.

questions.question:
A spill of sulfuric acid was neutralised by adding solid sodium acetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) in excess. Weak bases are typically used to safely neutralise spills because they can be used in excess.

The equilibrium constants for sodium acetate / the acetate ion are:

| $K_{sp}$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) | $K_b$ ($\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$) |
|---|---|
| 210 | $5.6 \times 10^{-10}$ |

Assuming the products of neutralisation have a negligible impact on the system, determine the pH of the solution once sodium acetate no longer dissolves.
questions.answer:
When no more dissolves the solution is saturated:

$\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{Na}^+(aq)$, $\quad K_{sp} = [\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-][\text{Na}^+] = x^2 = 210$

$x = \sqrt{210} = 14.49$, so $[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-] = 14.49$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Hydrolysis of acetate: $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)$

$$K_b = \frac{[\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}][\text{OH}^-]}{[\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-]} = \frac{y^2}{14.49 - y} = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$$

Assuming $y \ll 14.49$: $y^2 = 14.49 \times 5.6 \times 10^{-10} = 8.115 \times 10^{-9}$, so $y = [\text{OH}^-] = 9.01 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$.

$\text{pOH} = -\log_{10}(9.01 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.05$, so $\text{pH} = 14 - 4.05 = 9.95$.

questions.question:
A student tested the properties of potassium dihydrogen phosphate. She wrote the following observations as part of her testing.

> *Solid potassium dihydrogen phosphate was added to a solution of HCl. An increase in pH was observed.*
>
> *Solid potassium dihydrogen phosphate was added to a solution of NaOH. A decrease in pH was observed.*

Explain the student's observations.
questions.answer:
Potassium dihydrogen phosphate ($\text{KH}_2\text{PO}_4$) dissolves to give $\text{K}^+$ and the dihydrogen phosphate ion, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$, which is **amphiprotic** — it can act as a Brønsted–Lowry base (proton acceptor) or acid (proton donor).

- In HCl (strongly acidic), $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as a base, accepting protons:
  $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
  This reduces $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$, so the pH increases.
- In NaOH (strongly basic), $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as an acid, donating a proton to hydroxide:
  $$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
  This reduces $[\text{OH}^-]$, so the pH decreases.

So the observations are explained by the amphiprotic nature of the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ ion.

questions.question:
A student proposed a five-step synthesis pathway to convert but-1-ene into a product, as outlined in the flowchart:

but-1-ene $\xrightarrow{\text{i}}$ butane $\xrightarrow{\text{ii}}$ 1-bromobutane $\xrightarrow{\text{iii}}$ butan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\text{iv}}$ butanoic acid; then butanoic acid + Compound Y $\xrightarrow{\text{v}}$ the ester shown, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.

Identify the reactants and conditions for reaction i (but-1-ene → butane).
questions.answer:
Hydrogen gas ($\text{H}_2$) with a metal catalyst such as palladium on carbon (Pd/C), or Pt/Ni, with heat:
$$\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{H}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Pd/C}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$$

questions.question:
A student proposed a five-step synthesis pathway to convert but-1-ene into a product, as outlined in the flowchart:

but-1-ene $\xrightarrow{\text{i}}$ butane $\xrightarrow{\text{ii}}$ 1-bromobutane $\xrightarrow{\text{iii}}$ butan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\text{iv}}$ butanoic acid; then butanoic acid + Compound Y $\xrightarrow{\text{v}}$ the ester shown, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.

Identify the type of reaction for reaction iv (butan-1-ol → butanoic acid).
questions.answer: Oxidation (of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid, e.g. using acidified potassium dichromate or permanganate).

questions.question:
A student proposed a five-step synthesis pathway to convert but-1-ene into a product, as outlined in the flowchart:

but-1-ene $\xrightarrow{\text{i}}$ butane $\xrightarrow{\text{ii}}$ 1-bromobutane $\xrightarrow{\text{iii}}$ butan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\text{iv}}$ butanoic acid; then butanoic acid + Compound Y $\xrightarrow{\text{v}}$ the ester shown, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.

Provide the IUPAC name and draw the full structural formula for Compound Y.
questions.answer:
The ester is propan-2-yl butanoate: the alkyl group on the ester oxygen is $-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, so it came from the secondary alcohol **propan-2-ol**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ (esterification: butanoic acid + propan-2-ol ⇌ ester + water).

Full structural formula: a three-carbon chain with the –OH on the middle carbon (all other bonds to H), as shown.

questions.question:
A student proposed a five-step synthesis pathway to convert but-1-ene into a product, as outlined in the flowchart:

but-1-ene $\xrightarrow{\text{i}}$ butane $\xrightarrow{\text{ii}}$ 1-bromobutane $\xrightarrow{\text{iii}}$ butan-1-ol $\xrightarrow{\text{iv}}$ butanoic acid; then butanoic acid + Compound Y $\xrightarrow{\text{v}}$ the ester shown, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH(CH}_3)_2$.

Assuming but-1-ene remains the starting reagent, explain one limitation of this reaction pathway and propose a modification to address it. Support your answer with a balanced chemical equation.
questions.answer:
**Limitation:** reaction ii is a free-radical substitution of butane with bromine in UV light:
$$\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + \text{Br}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{UV}} \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br} + \text{HBr}$$
This reaction is difficult to control: Br can replace an H on either C1 or C2, giving a mixture of 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane, and further substitution gives dibromo- and polybromo-butanes. The yield of the required 1-bromobutane is therefore low and the product must be separated from the by-products. (Steps i and ii also hydrogenate the double bond only to put a functional group back on — the pathway is long, and every extra step lowers the overall yield.)

**Modification:** use a large excess of butane relative to bromine and limited exposure to UV to minimise multiple substitution, then separate the 1-bromobutane (b.p. 101 °C) from 2-bromobutane (b.p. 91 °C) and polybrominated by-products by fractional distillation before step iii, so that pure 1-bromobutane is carried forward to give pure butan-1-ol and butanoic acid.

*Note:* the paper's sample answer proposed replacing steps i–ii with $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}$ to make 1-bromobutane, but by Markovnikov's rule the major product of HBr addition to but-1-ene is **2-bromobutane**, so on its own this would not give the required 1-bromobutane in good yield.

questions.question:
Chemists often test starting reagents to ensure they have been supplied with the correct substance.

Propose a chemical test and the expected results to determine that a starting reagent is but-1-ene, rather than butane.
questions.answer:
Add a few drops of bromine water to a sample of the reagent and shake, **in the dark** (no UV light).

- But-1-ene (an alkene) rapidly **decolourises** the orange-brown bromine water, because $\text{Br}_2$ adds across the C=C double bond: $\text{CH}_2{=}\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{CH}_2\text{BrCHBrCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
- Butane (an alkane) does **not** decolourise bromine water in the absence of UV light — the orange-brown colour remains.

(Acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ could also be used: purple → colourless with but-1-ene, no change with butane.)

questions.question:
As part of a first-hand investigation relating to the fermentation of glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$), students added yeast to a solution of glucose, then plugged the top of the flask with cotton wool.

The apparatus was left at 30 °C for 45 hours.

The graph shows the change in mass of the flask over the 45-hour period: the mass falls steeply from 150 g at first, then more and more slowly, and becomes constant at about 140 g after about 30 hours.

Analysis of the reaction mixture after the 45 hours indicated the presence of unreacted glucose.

With the support of a balanced chemical equation, explain the shape of the graph.
questions.answer:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq) \xrightarrow{\text{yeast}} 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq) + 2\text{CO}_2(g)$$

- **Mass decreases:** fermentation produces carbon dioxide gas, which escapes through the cotton wool plug, so the mass of the flask falls.
- **Steep initial decrease:** at the start the glucose concentration is high, so the rate of fermentation (and of $\text{CO}_2$ loss) is high.
- **Gradually flattening curve:** as glucose is consumed its concentration decreases and ethanol accumulates, so the rate of reaction falls and the mass decreases more slowly.
- **Constant mass (after ~30 h):** the reaction stops even though glucose remains. Fermentation stops when the ethanol concentration becomes high enough (about 14–15%) to kill/inhibit the yeast, so no more $\text{CO}_2$ is produced and the mass stays at about 140 g.

questions.question:
Vitamin C, also known as ascorbic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$), is one of the most common supplements in the world.

It is titrated using an iodine ($\text{I}_2$) standard solution to a blue-black starch–iodine endpoint:

$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6(aq) + \text{I}_2(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{I}^-(aq) + \text{C}_6\text{H}_6\text{O}_6(aq) + 2\text{H}^+(aq)$$

An analytical chemist determined the vitamin C composition in a tablet using the following method:

1. A 1.500 g tablet was crushed in a mortar and pestle and dissolved in 200.0 mL of distilled water.
2. 20.00 mL of the solution was pipetted into a 250 mL conical flask with a few drops of starch indicator.
3. It was titrated using 0.005000 mol L$^{-1}$ iodine solution until 3 concordant results were achieved.

The average titre was recorded as 23.35 mL.

Determine the percentage (w/w) of vitamin C in the tablet.

The structures of propanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), propanamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$) and propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) are shown (left to right).

The properties of the three substances are displayed below.

| Substance | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| pH | 8 | 3 | 11 |
| Boiling point (°C) | 213 | 141 | 51 |

Determine the identity of each substance and analyse the differences in pH and boiling point.
questions.answer:
**A = propanamide, B = propanoic acid, C = propanamine.**

**pH:**
- Propanoic acid (B, pH 3) is a weak acid: the –COOH group partially ionises, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^- + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$.
- Propanamine (C, pH 11) is a weak base: the lone pair on the N atom accepts a proton, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-$.
- Propanamide (A, pH 8) is close to neutral: the N lone pair is drawn towards (delocalised onto) the electronegative carbonyl oxygen, so it is far less available to accept a proton than in the amine.

**Boiling point:** all three have similar-sized molecules (similar dispersion forces), so the differences come from hydrogen bonding.
- Propanamine (51 °C) has the lowest boiling point: N–H···N hydrogen bonds are relatively weak because N is less electronegative than O, and there is no C=O group.
- Propanoic acid (141 °C) forms strong O–H···O hydrogen bonds; molecules pair up into hydrogen-bonded **dimers**, roughly doubling the effective size and dispersion forces.
- Propanamide (213 °C) has the highest boiling point: its –CONH$_2$ group has two N–H hydrogen-bond donors plus a very polar C=O acceptor, so each molecule forms an extensive network of hydrogen bonds (not just dimers) — the strongest overall intermolecular forces.

questions.question:
The structures of propanamine ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), propanamide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CONH}_2$) and propanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) are shown (left to right).

Identify relevant features of the infrared spectra that could be used to distinguish between the molecules.
questions.answer:
- **Propanoic acid:** a very broad, strong O–H (acid) absorption at about 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$, and a strong, sharp C=O absorption at about 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$.
- **Propanamide:** also a strong C=O absorption at about 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$, but instead of the broad acid O–H it shows N–H absorptions at about 3300–3500 cm$^{-1}$ (narrower than the acid O–H band).
- **Propanamine:** N–H absorption at about 3300–3500 cm$^{-1}$ but **no** C=O absorption around 1700 cm$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
Two separate conductivity titrations were performed by gradually adding 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH to separate 25.0 mL samples of 0.2 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid (HCl) and hydrofluoric acid (HF).

The volume of NaOH added was recorded against the conductivity of the solution, producing the two conductivity curves shown. (HCl: starts at about 9.6 units, falls in a straight line to a minimum of about 0.6 at 50 mL, then rises to about 8 at 100 mL. HF: starts at about 6, falls less steeply to a minimum of about 2.3 at 50 mL, then rises to about 8.5 at 100 mL.)

Explain the similarities and differences in the conductivity curves for the two acids. Include relevant equations to support your answer.
questions.answer:
**Similarities**
- Both acids are monoprotic and react with NaOH in a 1 : 1 ratio:
  $\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$;
  $\text{HF}(aq) + \text{NaOH}(aq) \rightarrow \text{NaF}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$.
- Both contain $n = 0.2 \times 0.0250 = 5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol of acid, so both need $5.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol NaOH $= 50$ mL of 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH — both minima (equivalence points) occur at 50 mL.
- Before equivalence, both conductivities fall as highly mobile $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions are neutralised ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and replaced by much less mobile $\text{Na}^+$ ions.
- After equivalence, both rise at a similar rate because excess $\text{Na}^+$ and highly mobile $\text{OH}^-$ ions accumulate.

**Differences**
- HCl starts at higher conductivity: it is a strong acid and fully ionised, $\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{Cl}^-$. HF is a weak acid that only partially ionises, $\text{HF} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{F}^-$, so there are fewer ions initially.
- The HF curve falls less steeply: as $\text{OH}^-$ removes $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, more HF ionises, and each HF neutralised is replaced by $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{F}^-$ ions, partly offsetting the loss of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$.
- At equivalence the HF solution's conductivity is higher than the HCl solution's: the $\text{F}^-$ ion is a weak base and hydrolyses, $\text{F}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HF} + \text{OH}^-$, adding some mobile $\text{OH}^-$, whereas $\text{Cl}^-$ does not hydrolyse (the HCl solution is just $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Cl}^-$ and water).

*Note:* the paper's sample answer gave the equivalence point as 25 mL in one place (it is 50 mL, as on the graph) and attributed the higher HF minimum to $\text{F}^-$ being "smaller and therefore more mobile"; in fact hydrated $\text{F}^-$ is *less* mobile than $\text{Cl}^-$, so that explanation is incorrect.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name for the structure shown?
questions.answer: The molecule is an amide of methanoic acid ($\text{HCONR}_2$, a C=O bonded to N), and the nitrogen carries two methyl groups, each needing its own locant: $N,N$-dimethylmethanamide.

questions.question: Which of the following compounds is produced in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and calcium carbonate but **not** in the reaction between hydrochloric acid and calcium hydroxide?
questions.answer: $\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$, whereas $\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Only the carbonate gives carbon dioxide.

questions.question:
What is the equilibrium expression for the equilibrium system shown?

$$\text{Fe}_3\text{O}_4(s) + 4\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 3\text{Fe}(s) + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$$
questions.answer: Pure solids are omitted from the equilibrium expression, and each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient: $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[\text{H}_2\text{O}]^4}{[\text{H}_2]^4}$.

questions.question: Which of the following substances is an Arrhenius base?
questions.answer: An Arrhenius base produces hydroxide ions by dissociation in water. $\text{Sr(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Sr}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-$ contains $\text{OH}^-$ ions; the others are bases only in the Brønsted–Lowry sense (they accept protons).

questions.question: Which compound listed below will react in the presence of concentrated sulfuric acid with the product of its own oxidation to produce an ester?
questions.answer: Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol, so it oxidises (via propanal) to propanoic acid. The alcohol and the acid then esterify (conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst) to give propyl propanoate. Propan-2-ol oxidises to a ketone, which cannot form an ester; propanal and propanoic acid are not alcohols.

questions.question: Which compound will produce a peak at 210 ppm in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR spectroscopy?
questions.answer: Carbonyl carbons of aldehydes and ketones appear at about 190–220 ppm. Pentanal's CHO carbon gives the peak near 210 ppm (a carboxylic acid C=O is lower, about 160–185 ppm; C–O and C–N carbons are about 25–70 ppm).

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium system shown for the production of nitrosyl chloride (NOCl).

$$2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NOCl}(g) \qquad \Delta H = -75.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which of the following conditions will maximise the equilibrium yield of nitrosyl chloride?
questions.answer: The forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles (3 → 2), so high pressure shifts equilibrium right (Le Chatelier). The forward reaction is exothermic, so low temperature also shifts equilibrium right.

questions.question:
The titration curve below shows the pH as titrant is added (equivalence point at about 25 mL; the pH starts near 3, rises slowly through a buffer region to about 6, jumps to about 11, then levels off near 12.5).

Which of the following titrations would result in this titration curve?
options: 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH
0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH
0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl with 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ $\text{NH}_3$
questions.answer: The starting pH (~3) and the gradual buffer region before equivalence show a weak acid (propanoic acid); the high final pH (~12.5) and the equivalence point above 7 show a strong base (NaOH). A strong acid would start near pH 1, and ammonia would not take the pH above about 11.

questions.question:
The titration curve below shows the pH as titrant is added (equivalence point at about 25 mL; the pH starts near 3, rises slowly through a buffer region to about 6, jumps to about 11, then levels off near 12.5).

Which of the following indicators is most suitable for determining the endpoint of this titration?
questions.answer: The vertical section of the curve (equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration) is at about pH 7–11, centred around pH 8–9. Phenolphthalein changes colour within this range.

questions.question: An aqueous solution containing which substance is most likely to have a pH of 9?
questions.answer: Amines are weak bases: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-$, giving a basic solution. Methanol and butanal are neutral; propanoic acid is acidic.

questions.question: In proton NMR, what do the relative peak areas indicate about a pure substance?
options: The number of protons in the molecule.
The ratio of protons in different environments.
The proximity of the proton to an electronegative element.
The molecular weight of the molecule.
questions.answer: Peak area (integration) is proportional to the number of hydrogens in each environment, so the relative areas give the ratio of protons in the different environments (not the absolute number). Proximity to electronegative atoms affects chemical shift instead.

questions.question: Infrared spectroscopy of a pure compound produces a broad peak centred at 3415 cm$^{-1}$. Which series of organic compounds is the unknown compound likely to belong to?
questions.answer: A broad absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ is the hydrogen-bonded O–H stretch of an alcohol. A carboxylic acid O–H is much broader and lower (about 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$).

questions.question: Which of the following mixtures of aqueous species will form a buffer solution when both species have a concentration of approximately 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$?
questions.answer: A buffer is a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts. Methanoic acid is a weak acid and methanoate is its conjugate base. HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ is not an effective base.

questions.question:
The graph shows changes in the reaction quotient $Q$ over time for the equilibrium system

$$\text{X}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{Y}(g) \qquad \Delta H > 0$$

At $t_1$, $Q$ (already at equilibrium) begins to rise gradually from its equilibrium value to a new, higher constant value. At $t_2$, $Q$ drops suddenly, then rises gradually back to the same value it had just before $t_2$.

Which of the following could be the changes made at $t_1$ and $t_2$?
options: $t_1$: decrease in temperature; $t_2$: addition of X
$t_1$: decrease in temperature; $t_2$: removal of X
$t_1$: increase in temperature; $t_2$: addition of Y
$t_1$: increase in temperature; $t_2$: removal of Y
questions.answer: $Q = \dfrac{[\text{Y}]}{[\text{X}]}$. At $t_1$ there is no sudden change, but $Q$ settles at a higher value, so $K_{eq}$ increased: for an endothermic reaction this means the temperature was increased. At $t_2$, $Q$ suddenly falls and returns to the same value (same $K_{eq}$, so same temperature): a concentration change that lowers $[\text{Y}]/[\text{X}]$, i.e. removal of Y (or addition of X — but addition of X is not paired with a temperature increase in the options).

questions.question: Which set of peaks would be likely found in the mass spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropanal?
questions.answer: 2,2-Dimethylpropanal is $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CHO}$, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$, $M = 86$ (molecular ion at 86). Likely fragments: $\text{CH}_3^+$ (15), $\text{CHO}^+$ (29), $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^+$ (57) and $[M-\text{CH}_3]^+$ (71).

questions.question: Which infrared spectrum was most likely produced from a pure sample of propanone?
questions.answer: Propanone has a C=O but no O–H. Spectrum C shows a very strong C=O absorption near 1715 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H near 3000 cm$^{-1}$ with no O–H band. A has a sharp O–H (free) band near 3600 cm$^{-1}$, B a broad O–H band (alcohol), and D has no strong C=O peak.

questions.question:
In an experiment to determine the $K_{sp}$ value of barium fluoride, 1.0 mL samples containing barium ions were each added to a 1.0 mL solution containing fluoride ions. The results are given below.

| Sample | Initial [Ba$^{2+}$] (mol L$^{-1}$), volume 1.0 mL | Initial [F$^-$] (mol L$^{-1}$), volume 1.0 mL | Observation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.010 | 0.026 | No precipitate |
| 2 | 0.010 | 0.028 | No precipitate |
| 3 | 0.010 | 0.030 | Faint white precipitate |
| 4 | 0.010 | 0.032 | White precipitate |

Which of the following could be the $K_{sp}$ value of barium fluoride?
questions.answer: Mixing halves each concentration: $[\text{Ba}^{2+}] = 0.0050$. Sample 2: $[\text{F}^-] = 0.014$, $Q = 0.0050 \times 0.014^2 = 9.8 \times 10^{-7}$ (no precipitate, so $K_{sp} > 9.8 \times 10^{-7}$). Sample 3: $[\text{F}^-] = 0.015$, $Q = 0.0050 \times 0.015^2 = 1.1 \times 10^{-6}$ (precipitate, so $K_{sp} \le 1.1 \times 10^{-6}$). Only $1.0 \times 10^{-6}$ lies in this range.

questions.question: When ethene is reacted completely with hydrogen bromide, 7.27 L of the product is obtained at 25.0 °C and 120 kPa. What is the mass of ethene that was reacted?
questions.answer: $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + \text{HBr} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}$ (1 : 1). Treating the product as a gas: $n = \dfrac{PV}{RT} = \dfrac{120 \times 7.27}{8.314 \times 298.15} = 0.352$ mol. $m(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4) = 0.352 \times 28.05 = 9.87$ g.

questions.question: A salt has a $K_{sp}$ value of $4.3 \times 10^{-10}$ and a molar solubility of $2.0 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$. Which of the following represents the formula of this salt?

1.242 kg of a single polymer with the repeating unit shown below (–O–CH₂CH₂–O–CO–C₆H₄–CO–, i.e. a polyester of ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) was obtained after a polymerisation reaction.

What mass of water is released during this polymerisation reaction?
questions.answer: Repeating unit $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$, $M = 192.2$ g mol$^{-1}$. $n(\text{units}) = \dfrac{1242}{192.2} = 6.46$ mol. Each repeating unit contains two ester links, so 2 water molecules are released per unit: $n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = 12.9$ mol, $m = 12.9 \times 18.02 = 233$ g.

questions.question: Using balanced chemical equations, show that the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ ion can react with both strong acids and strong bases.
questions.answer:
With a strong acid ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as a base, accepting a proton):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{H}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4(aq)$$
With a strong base ($\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ acts as an acid, donating a proton):
$$\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$$
So $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is amphiprotic. ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ or a named strong acid such as HCl, and any metal hydroxide, are equally acceptable.)

questions.question: Calculate the pH of 0.20 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrazoic acid ($\text{HN}_3$, $K_a = 1.9 \times 10^{-5}$).
questions.answer:
$\text{HN}_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+(aq) + \text{N}_3^-(aq)$

| | $\text{HN}_3$ | $\text{H}^+$ | $\text{N}_3^-$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | 0.20 | 0 | 0 |
| C | $-x$ | $+x$ | $+x$ |
| E | $0.20 - x$ | $x$ | $x$ |

$K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{N}_3^-]}{[\text{HN}_3]} = \dfrac{x^2}{0.20 - x} \approx \dfrac{x^2}{0.20} = 1.9 \times 10^{-5}$ (assuming $x \ll 0.20$)

$x^2 = 3.8 \times 10^{-6}$, so $x = [\text{H}^+] = 1.9 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L$^{-1}$

$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.9 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.71$ (the same result is obtained without the approximation).

questions.question:
Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

Give the equilibrium expression for this reaction.
questions.answer: $$K_{eq} = \frac{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}{[\text{HI}]^2}$$

questions.question:
Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

In an experiment, 1.75 mol of hydrogen iodide was placed in a 1.00 L vessel at a constant temperature. At equilibrium, the concentration of iodine gas was 0.168 mol L$^{-1}$.

What is the $K_{eq}$ value at this temperature?

Hydrogen iodide decomposes when heated to hydrogen and iodine:

$$2\text{HI}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g)$$

Explain what would happen to the value of $K_{eq}$ if a catalyst was added at constant temperature.
questions.answer: $K_{eq}$ stays the same. A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing the rates of the forward and reverse reactions by the same factor. The forward and reverse rates therefore stay equal, the equilibrium concentrations of $\text{H}_2$, $\text{I}_2$ and HI are unchanged (equilibrium is simply reached faster), so $K_{eq}$ is unchanged.

questions.question:
100.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide is mixed with 100.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ nitric acid in a cardboard cup. The initial temperature of each solution is 24.30 °C and the resulting solution has a temperature of 31.15 °C.

You can assume that there is no volume change upon reaction, and that the resulting solution has a density of 1.04 g mL$^{-1}$ and a specific heat capacity of 4.03 J K$^{-1}$ g$^{-1}$.

Calculate the enthalpy of neutralisation for this reaction.
questions.answer:
$m(\text{solution}) = 200.0\ \text{mL} \times 1.04\ \text{g mL}^{-1} = 208\ \text{g}$

$\Delta T = 31.15 - 24.30 = 6.85\ \text{K}$

$q = mc\Delta T = 208 \times 4.03 \times 6.85 = 5740\ \text{J} = 5.74\ \text{kJ}$

$n(\text{H}_2\text{O}) = n(\text{HNO}_3) = n(\text{NaOH}) = 1.00 \times 0.1000 = 0.100\ \text{mol}$

$\Delta H = -\dfrac{5.74\ \text{kJ}}{0.100\ \text{mol}} = -57.4\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ (negative because the reaction is exothermic).

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Plot this data on a graph of $K_{eq}$ against temperature, including a curved line of best fit.
questions.answer:
Plot temperature (K) on the horizontal axis (e.g. 380–450 K) and $K_{eq}$ on the vertical axis (e.g. 0–100), with labelled axes and an even scale that uses most of the grid. Plot the five points (390, 90), (400, 44), (420, 12), (430, 6.4), (440, 3.6) accurately and draw a smooth curve through them: $K_{eq}$ falls steeply at first, then levels off, approaching zero at higher temperatures (a decaying curve, concave up).

Marking: correct labelled axes, appropriate scale (graph uses at least 25% of each axis), accurate plotting, smooth curve through all points.

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Using a graph of this data with a curved line of best fit, estimate $K_{eq}$ at 410 K.
questions.answer: Reading from the curve at 410 K (between 44 at 400 K and 12 at 420 K, the curve sagging below the straight line joining them): $K_{eq} \approx 23$ (values of about 22–27 read from a reasonable curve are accepted).

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

At 410 K, $K_{eq}$ is approximately 23. A system at 410 K is found to have $[\text{N}_2] = 0.24$ mol L$^{-1}$, $[\text{H}_2] = 1.1$ mol L$^{-1}$ and $[\text{NH}_3] = 1.6$ mol L$^{-1}$.

Show that this system is not at equilibrium and use $Q$ and $K_{eq}$ to explain how the system will shift to reach equilibrium.
questions.answer:
$$Q = \frac{[\text{NH}_3]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3} = \frac{(1.6)^2}{(0.24)(1.1)^3} = \frac{2.56}{0.319} = 8.0$$

$Q \neq K_{eq}$ ($Q \approx 8 < K_{eq} \approx 23$), so the system is not at equilibrium.

For $Q$ to increase to $K_{eq}$, the forward reaction is favoured: $[\text{NH}_3]$ increases while $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$ decrease, until $Q = K_{eq}$.

questions.question:
The synthesis of ammonia from its elements is an equilibrium process:

$$\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$$

The table shows the value of $K_{eq}$ for this reaction at a range of temperatures.

| Temperature (K) | 390 | 400 | 420 | 430 | 440 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $K_{eq}$ | 90 | 44 | 12 | 6.4 | 3.6 |

Is the production of ammonia exothermic or endothermic? Justify your answer using Le Châtelier's principle and the data provided.
questions.answer:
The forward reaction (production of ammonia) is exothermic.

The data show that as temperature increases, $K_{eq}$ decreases (from 90 at 390 K to 3.6 at 440 K). A smaller $K_{eq}$ means the equilibrium mixture contains relatively less $\text{NH}_3$ and more $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$, i.e. the reverse reaction is favoured at higher temperature.

By Le Châtelier's principle, increasing the temperature favours the endothermic direction (which absorbs the added heat). Since the reverse reaction is favoured, the reverse reaction is endothermic and so the forward reaction, producing ammonia, is exothermic.

questions.question:
Soap can be used as a cleaning agent due to its ability to stabilise emulsions.

Draw a labelled diagram to show the structure of a soap molecule.
questions.answer: A soap is the salt of a long-chain fatty acid, e.g. sodium stearate $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_{16}\text{COO}^-\ \text{Na}^+$. The diagram shows a long hydrocarbon tail labelled **non-polar / hydrophobic end**, attached to a negatively charged carboxylate head ($-\text{COO}^-$) labelled **ionic / polar / hydrophilic end**.

questions.question:
Soap can be used as a cleaning agent due to its ability to stabilise emulsions.

Explain how soap can act as a cleaning agent.
questions.answer:
Grease and oil are non-polar and do not dissolve in water. When soap is added, the non-polar hydrocarbon tails of the soap anions dissolve in the grease, attracted by dispersion forces, while the ionic carboxylate heads remain in the water, attracted to water molecules by ion–dipole forces (and hydrogen bonding).

The soap anions surround small droplets of grease to form **micelles**: the grease is in the centre, and the outside of each micelle is covered in negatively charged heads. Because the micelles all carry a negative surface charge they repel each other and do not coalesce, so the grease is held as a stable emulsion of droplets suspended in the water. The emulsified grease is then washed away with the rinse water, cleaning the surface.

questions.question:
Two esters, A and B, have molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$. Ester A is ethyl propanoate ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, first structure) and ester B is *tert*-butyl methanoate ($\text{HCOOC(CH}_3)_3$, second structure). Their proton NMR data are:

**Ester A**

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 1.05 | 3 | triplet |
| 1.16 | 3 | triplet |
| 2.26 | 2 | quartet |
| 4.11 | 2 | quartet |

**Ester B**

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting |
|---|---|---|
| 1.42 | 9 | singlet |
| 9.60 | 1 | singlet |

State **two** differences between the proton NMR data and relate these to the structure of the two esters.
questions.answer:
**Difference 1 – number of peaks.** Ester A gives 4 peaks but ester B gives only 2. A has four different hydrogen environments (two different $\text{CH}_3$ groups and two different $\text{CH}_2$ groups, one next to C=O and one next to O), whereas in B the three methyl groups of the *tert*-butyl group are equivalent (one environment, 9H) and the other environment is the single H on the HCO group.

**Difference 2 – splitting pattern.** Ester A gives two triplets and two quartets, while ester B gives two singlets. In A each $\text{CH}_3$ is next to a $\text{CH}_2$ (2 neighbouring H → triplet) and each $\text{CH}_2$ is next to a $\text{CH}_3$ (3 neighbouring H → quartet), i.e. A contains two ethyl ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$–) groups. In B the methyl groups are attached to a quaternary carbon with no hydrogens, and the HCO hydrogen is attached to a carbon with no H neighbours, so both sets of protons are isolated and appear as singlets.

(Other valid differences: B has a peak at 9.60 ppm from the H on the carbonyl carbon (H–C=O), which A lacks; the peak-area ratios are 3:3:2:2 for A but 9:1 for B.)

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

By performing a relevant calculation, show that Solution X is the 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.
questions.answer:
HCl is a strong acid and fully ionises, so $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 0.0600$ mol L$^{-1}$:
$$\text{pH} = -\log_{10}(0.0600) = 1.22$$
This equals the initial pH of solution X, so X is the 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ HCl.

(Alternatively: $n(\text{HCl}) = 0.006$ mol, $n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.001$ mol, excess HCl $= 0.005$ mol in 0.101 L, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 0.0495$ mol L$^{-1}$, pH $= 1.31$ = final pH of X.)

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

Calculate the $K_a$ of the weak acid.
questions.answer:
Solution Y is the buffer with $[\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]$. Since $K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$, when $[\text{HA}] = [\text{A}^-]$, $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = K_a$, so $\text{p}K_a = \text{pH} = 4.76$.
$$K_a = 10^{-4.76} = 1.7 \times 10^{-5}$$

questions.question:
The pH of two 100 mL solutions, X and Y, was measured before and after 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution was added to each.

| | Initial pH | Final pH |
|---|---|---|
| Solution X | 1.22 | 1.31 |
| Solution Y | 4.76 | 4.84 |

One of these solutions contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, both at a concentration of 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$; the other contains a 0.060 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrochloric acid.

When 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution is added to 100 mL of water, the pH increases from 7.00 to 12.00.

Explain why adding 1.00 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide solution to both solution X and solution Y does not change the pH of either appreciably.
questions.answer:
Both solutions receive $n(\text{OH}^-) = 1.00 \times 0.00100 = 1.00$ mmol.

**Solution X:** contains $100\ \text{mL} \times 0.0600 = 6.00$ mmol HCl. After neutralising 1.00 mmol, 5.00 mmol of HCl remains, so the strong acid is still present in large excess; $[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]$ falls only slightly (0.0600 → 0.0495 mol L$^{-1}$) and the pH rises only from 1.22 to 1.31.

**Solution Y:** is a buffer containing 10.0 mmol of the weak acid HA and 10.0 mmol of its conjugate base A$^-$. The added hydroxide reacts with the weak acid: $\text{HA} + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{A}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving 9.00 mmol HA and 11.00 mmol A$^-$. The added OH$^-$ is consumed rather than remaining free in solution, and the ratio $[\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}]$ stays close to 1, so the pH stays close to the p$K_a$ (4.76 → 4.84).

questions.question:
Linalool (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol) is a compound found in many flowers and spices. Its structural formula is shown: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

State the names of the **two** functional groups in linalool.
questions.answer:
1. Alkene (carbon–carbon double bond)
2. Alcohol (hydroxyl group) — specifically a tertiary alcohol.

questions.question:
Linalool (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-ol) is a compound found in many flowers and spices. Its structural formula is shown: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

Draw the structural formula of the organic product formed when linalool reacts with each of the following reagents under the stated conditions:

1. $\text{H}_2(g)$, Pd catalyst
2. $\text{Br}_2(aq)$
3. $\text{HCOOH}(aq)$, $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst, heated under reflux
questions.answer:
1. **$\text{H}_2$/Pd:** both C=C double bonds are hydrogenated, the OH is unchanged: 3,7-dimethyloctan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH(CH}_3)_2$.
2. **$\text{Br}_2$:** bromine adds across both double bonds: 1,2,6,7-tetrabromo-3,7-dimethyloctan-3-ol, $\text{CH}_2\text{Br-CHBr-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CHBr-CBr(CH}_3)_2$.
3. **HCOOH / $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / reflux:** esterification of the OH group with methanoic acid (both C=C remain): linalyl methanoate (3,7-dimethylocta-1,6-dien-3-yl methanoate), $\text{H-CO-O-C(CH}_3\text{)(CH=CH}_2\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-CH=C(CH}_3)_2$.

questions.question:
The compound responsible for the hot taste of chillies, capsaicin, is shown. It has a long hydrocarbon chain attached through an amide group to a benzene ring bearing –OH and –OCH₃ groups. Drinking full cream milk, which contains fat, is recommended after eating meals containing lots of chilli as it reduces the hot taste on the tongue.

Explain why milk is better than water in removing capsaicin from the tongue.
questions.answer:
Although capsaicin has some polar groups (–OH, –O–, amide), most of the molecule is a large non-polar hydrocarbon chain and benzene ring, so overall it is largely non-polar. It cannot form enough hydrogen bonds / dipole–dipole attractions with water to overcome the strong hydrogen bonding between water molecules, so it is only very slightly soluble in water and water does not remove it from the tongue.

Full cream milk contains fat, which is non-polar. The non-polar parts of capsaicin form dispersion forces with the fat molecules, comparable in strength to those between capsaicin molecules, so capsaicin dissolves readily in the fat (milk is also an emulsion of fat droplets stabilised by emulsifiers, which can take up capsaicin). Capsaicin is therefore far more soluble in milk than in water, and milk carries it away from the tongue.

questions.question:
Three bottles, known to contain pentan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol, are missing labels.

Suggest how a student could distinguish between the three alcohols using one or more chemical tests.
questions.answer:
Warm a sample of each alcohol with acidified potassium dichromate solution.
- 2-methylbutan-2-ol (tertiary) is not oxidised: the solution stays orange.
- Pentan-1-ol (primary) and pentan-3-ol (secondary) are oxidised: the solution turns from orange to green.

To distinguish these two, heat each under reflux with excess acidified dichromate, then test the product with sodium carbonate solution. Pentan-1-ol is oxidised to pentanoic acid, which gives effervescence ($\text{CO}_2$ bubbles); pentan-3-ol is oxidised to pentan-3-one, a ketone, which gives no effervescence.

(Alternative accepted: Lucas reagent — the tertiary alcohol turns cloudy immediately, the secondary turns cloudy after some minutes, and the primary remains a clear, colourless solution.)

questions.question:
Three bottles, known to contain pentan-1-ol, pentan-3-ol and 2-methylbutan-2-ol, are missing labels.

The student can use a combination of infrared spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR to confirm the contents of the three bottles. Evaluate the suitability of these techniques for this purpose.
questions.answer:
**Infrared spectroscopy — not suitable on its own.** All three compounds are alcohols with an O–H group, so all would show a broad O–H absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$ and C–H and C–O absorptions. The spectra would differ only subtly in the fingerprint region, so IR confirms that each bottle contains an alcohol but cannot reliably identify which isomer is which.

**Mass spectrometry — limited suitability.** The three alcohols are isomers ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$) with the same molar mass, so all give a molecular ion peak at $m/z = 88$. Fragmentation patterns differ somewhat, but the molecular ion alone cannot distinguish them.

**$^{13}\text{C}$ NMR — highly suitable.** Each alcohol has a different number of carbon environments because of its symmetry:
- pentan-1-ol, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$: 5 environments → 5 peaks;
- pentan-3-ol, $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2)_2\text{CHOH}$: symmetrical → 3 peaks;
- 2-methylbutan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$: 4 environments → 4 peaks.

**Judgement:** $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR alone can identify each bottle; IR and MS are useful only to confirm the alcohol functional group and the molar mass, so the combination is suitable mainly because of the $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR data.

questions.question:
Alkene A reacts with gaseous hydrogen chloride to form two isomers, B and C, with molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Cl}$. A sequence of reactions for each compound is shown below:

- B → (substitution reaction using dilute NaOH(aq)) → D → (oxidation using acidified potassium dichromate solution) → **no reaction**
- C → (substitution reaction using dilute NaOH(aq)) → E → (oxidation using acidified potassium dichromate solution) → F

Determine the structural formulae of the compounds A to F.
questions.answer:
D is not oxidised, so it is a tertiary alcohol; the only tertiary $\text{C}_4$ alcohol is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, so the alkene must be branched.

- **A:** 2-methylpropene (methylpropene), $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)_2$
- **B:** 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}$
- **C:** 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Cl}$
- **D:** 2-methylpropan-2-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{COH}$ (tertiary, not oxidised)
- **E:** 2-methylpropan-1-ol, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{OH}$ (primary)
- **F:** 2-methylpropanoic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$ (2-methylpropanal, from partial oxidation, was also accepted)

(But-1-ene would give 2-chlorobutane and 1-chlorobutane, whose alcohols are secondary and primary — both oxidisable — so it does not fit.)

questions.question:
Periclase is a mineral composed of magnesium oxide ($M = 40.31$ g mol$^{-1}$). A 0.4802 g ore sample containing periclase is treated with 50.00 mL of 0.5020 mol L$^{-1}$ hydrochloric acid. The acid reacts with the magnesium oxide, but not with the other components of the ore sample. After reaction and filtration, the solution is made up to 250.0 mL in a volumetric flask. 25.00 mL aliquots of this solution are titrated with 0.1034 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide, requiring an average of 12.90 mL to reach the endpoint.

Calculate the percentage by mass of magnesium oxide in the periclase ore sample.
questions.answer:
$\text{MgO}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$; $\ \text{HCl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{HCl added}) = 0.05000 \times 0.5020 = 25.10$ mmol

$n(\text{NaOH}) = 0.01290 \times 0.1034 = 1.334$ mmol $= n(\text{HCl excess in aliquot})$

$n(\text{HCl excess, total}) = 1.334 \times \dfrac{250.0}{25.00} = 13.34$ mmol

$n(\text{HCl reacted with MgO}) = 25.10 - 13.34 = 11.76$ mmol

$n(\text{MgO}) = \dfrac{11.76}{2} = 5.881$ mmol

$m(\text{MgO}) = 5.881 \times 10^{-3} \times 40.31 = 0.2371$ g

$\%\text{MgO} = \dfrac{0.2371}{0.4802} \times 100 = 49.37\%$

$$\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + \text{SCN}^-(aq) \rightleftharpoons [\text{FeSCN}]^{2+}(aq)$$

At equilibrium at 298 K there are 0.00540 mol of $\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)$, 0.00823 mol of $\text{SCN}^-(aq)$ and 0.0631 mol of $[\text{FeSCN}]^{2+}(aq)$ in a 100.0 mL solution.

Compound Q is an organic compound which contains roughly 19% nitrogen by mass. The infrared, $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR and $^1\text{H}$ NMR spectra of compound Q are shown (in that order).

- IR: a weak, fairly sharp absorption near 3400 cm$^{-1}$; strong C–H absorptions just below 3000 cm$^{-1}$; no absorption near 1700 cm$^{-1}$.
- $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR: three peaks, at about 23, 35 and 50 ppm.
- $^1\text{H}$ NMR (relative areas): 3.25 ppm (1H, singlet), 2.9 ppm (1H, multiplet), 2.55 ppm (3H, singlet), 1.15 ppm (6H, doublet).

$^1\text{H}$ NMR chemical shift data:

| Type of proton | δ/ppm |
|---|---|
| R–CH$_3$ | 0.9–1.0 |
| R–CH$_2$–R | 1.2–1.5 |
| R–CHR$_2$ | 1.5–2.0 |
| R–C≡C–H | 2.0–3.1 |
| –CO–CH$_2$– (aldehydes, ketones, esters) | 2.1–2.7 |
| R–CH$_2$–NH$_2$ or CHR–NH$_2$ | 2.4–3.0 |
| R–CH$_2$–NHR or CHR–NHR | 2.5–3.1 |
| –CH$_2$–O– (alcohols, ethers, esters) | 3.3–4.8 |
| R–OH | 1–6 |
| R–NH$_2$ | 1–5 |
| R–NHR | 1–5 |
| R$_2$C=CHR (alkene) | 4.5–7.0 |
| R–CONH–R (amide) | 5–9 |
| R–CHO | 9.4–10.0 |
| R–COOH | 9.0–13.0 |

Draw and name compound Q and justify your choice using all the information provided.
questions.answer:
**Compound Q: $N$-methylpropan-2-amine**, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH-NH-CH}_3$.

**% composition:** if Q contains one N atom, $M \approx \dfrac{14.01}{0.19} \approx 74$ g mol$^{-1}$. The $^1$H NMR integrations total 11 H. Removing N and 11 H (25) from 74 leaves 49, about 4 C. Formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{11}\text{N}$ ($M = 73.14$; %N $= 19.2\%$ ✓), a saturated amine.

**IR:** the absorption near 3400 cm$^{-1}$ is an N–H stretch; a single weak peak suggests a secondary amine. There is no C=O (no peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$), so it is not an amide.

**$^{13}$C NMR:** only 3 peaks for 4 carbons, so two carbons are equivalent (symmetry). The peak at 50 ppm is in the C–N range (CH bonded to N), the 23 ppm peak is a C–C carbon (the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ of an isopropyl group), and the 35 ppm peak is the N–$\text{CH}_3$ carbon.

**$^1$H NMR:**
- 2.55 ppm, 3H singlet: a $\text{CH}_3$ with no neighbouring H, shifted into the 2.5–3.1 ppm range, so it is bonded to N: N–$\text{CH}_3$.
- 2.9 ppm, 1H multiplet: a CH bonded to N with many neighbouring H (six from two $\text{CH}_3$ groups → septet).
- 1.15 ppm, 6H doublet: two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups split by one neighbouring H. Together with the 1H multiplet this is an isopropyl group, $-\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$, bonded to N.
- 3.25 ppm, 1H singlet: the N–H proton (no splitting; within the 1–5 ppm range for R–NHR).

Putting the fragments together: $\text{CH}_3\text{-NH-CH(CH}_3)_2$, $N$-methylpropan-2-amine.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements correctly describes members of the same homologous series?

I. They undergo similar types of chemical reactions.
II. They contain the same functional group.
III. Consecutive members differ by a $-\mathrm{CH_2}-$ unit.

questions.answer: I, II and III are true. IV is false: e.g. methanol $\mathrm{CH_4O}$ and ethanol $\mathrm{C_2H_6O}$ have different empirical formulae.

questions.answer: Propan-1-ol has an O–H bond (strong, broad absorption at about 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$) and no C=O (no peak near 1700 cm$^{-1}$): spectrum A. (B and C have a strong C=O peak; D has no O–H absorption.)

questions.question:
An equilibrium exists between A, B and C.
$$\mathrm{A(g) + B(g) \rightleftharpoons 2C(g)} \qquad K_{eq} = 64 \text{ at 298 K}$$
When 5.0 moles of A is combined with 5.0 moles of B and added to a sealed 2.0 L flask, what is the concentration of C after reaching equilibrium?
questions.answer:
Initially $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = 2.5$ mol L$^{-1}$. At equilibrium $[\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{B}] = 2.5 - x$, $[\mathrm{C}] = 2x$:
$$\frac{(2x)^2}{(2.5 - x)^2} = 64 \Rightarrow \frac{2x}{2.5 - x} = 8 \Rightarrow x = 2.0,$$
so $[\mathrm{C}] = 4.0$ mol L$^{-1}$.

questions.question: Which of the following salts has the lowest solubility in g L$^{-1}$? (Use the $K_{sp}$ values on the HSC data sheet.)
questions.answer:
All four are 1:1 salts, so solubility $s = \sqrt{K_{sp}}$, then multiply by molar mass:
- $\mathrm{CuCO_3}$: $\sqrt{1.4 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$ × 123.6 = $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$ g L$^{-1}$
- $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$: $\sqrt{1.08 \times 10^{-10}} = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ mol L$^{-1}$ × 233.4 = $2.4 \times 10^{-3}$ g L$^{-1}$
- $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ and $\mathrm{PbSO_4}$ are much more soluble ($K_{sp}$ about $10^{-9}$ and $10^{-8}$).

Barium sulfate has the lowest molar solubility, but copper(II) carbonate is lowest in g L$^{-1}$ because of its smaller molar mass.

questions.question: A hydroxycarboxylic acid with the formula $\mathrm{HOCH_2CH_2COOH}$ ($M = 90$ g mol$^{-1}$) undergoes condensation polymerisation to form a polyester in which the average polymer chain contains 1200 monomer units. What is the approximate molar mass of an average polymer chain, in g mol$^{-1}$?
questions.answer:
Joining 1200 monomers releases 1199 water molecules:
$$1200 \times 90 - 1199 \times 18 \approx 86\,400 \text{ g mol}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: The titration curve shown was produced when NaOH solution was added to an acid. How many acidic protons does this acid possess?
questions.answer: There are two equivalence points (at about 10 mL and 20 mL), so the acid is diprotic: 2.

questions.question: The graph shows how the pH changes when sodium hydroxide solution is added to 15.0 mL of a 0.0288 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of a diprotic acid. What is the concentration of the sodium hydroxide solution?
questions.answer:
$n(\text{acid}) = 0.0288 \times 0.0150 = 4.32 \times 10^{-4}$ mol. The first equivalence point (10.0 mL) removes the first proton, so $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 4.32 \times 10^{-4}$ mol in 10.0 mL:
$$c = \frac{4.32 \times 10^{-4}}{0.0100} = 0.0432 \text{ mol L}^{-1}.$$

questions.question: Which of the following compounds will react fastest with Lucas' reagent (a saturated solution of zinc chloride in concentrated hydrochloric acid)?
questions.answer: Lucas' reagent substitutes Cl for OH; tertiary alcohols react fastest. B is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol. (A is primary, D secondary, and C is a ketone.)

questions.question:
The two equations and $K_{eq}$ values have been given for reactions involving NO(g).
$$\mathrm{N_2(g) + O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO(g)} \qquad K_{eq1} = 4.3 \times 10^{-31}$$
$$\mathrm{NO_2(g) \rightleftharpoons NO(g) + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2(g)} \qquad K_{eq2} = 7.4 \times 10^{-7}$$
What is the $K_{eq}$ value for the following reaction?
$$\mathrm{N_2(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)}$$
questions.answer:
Add equation 1 to twice the reverse of equation 2:
$$K_{eq} = K_{eq1} \times \left(\frac{1}{K_{eq2}}\right)^2 = \frac{4.3 \times 10^{-31}}{(7.4 \times 10^{-7})^2} \approx 7.9 \times 10^{-19}.$$

questions.question: The malonate ion, $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-}$, is classified as amphiprotic. Show, by writing two chemical equations, how this ion is amphiprotic.
questions.answer:
Acting as a base: $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + H_3O^+(aq) \rightarrow HOOCCH_2COOH(aq) + H_2O(l)}$

Acting as an acid: $\mathrm{HOOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow {}^-OOCCH_2COO^-(aq) + H_2O(l)}$

(Water is accepted as a reactant only in the equation where malonate acts as an acid.)

questions.question: Pent-2-ene can undergo polymerisation under suitable conditions. State the type of polymer produced from pent-2-ene.
questions.answer: An addition polymer.

questions.question: Pent-2-ene, $\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}CHCH_2CH_3}$, can undergo addition polymerisation. Draw a short section of the polymer produced, including two repeating units.
questions.answer:
The C=C opens and the two former double-bond carbons form the backbone, carrying a methyl and an ethyl side group:
$$-\mathrm{CH(CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_2CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_3)}-\mathrm{CH(CH_2CH_3)}-$$
i.e. a four-carbon section of backbone, with $-\mathrm{CH_3}$ on carbons 1 and 3 and $-\mathrm{CH_2CH_3}$ on carbons 2 and 4, and open bonds at each end.

questions.question: The boiling points of the first six compounds in the straight-chain carboxylic acid and primary amine series are shown in the plot. Explain the trends shown.
questions.answer:
**Trend 1:** boiling points increase as the number of C atoms increases in both series. Longer molecules have more electrons, so the dispersion forces between molecules are stronger and more energy is needed to overcome them.

**Trend 2:** carboxylic acids have higher boiling points than primary amines with the same number of carbon atoms. Both form hydrogen bonds, but O–H is more polar than N–H (O is more electronegative than N), so the hydrogen bonds between acid molecules are stronger (acids can also form dimers). More energy is needed to separate them.

**Trend 3:** the difference in boiling point between the two series becomes smaller as the chain gets longer. Dispersion forces grow with chain length while the hydrogen-bonding contribution of the functional group stays the same, so the functional group makes up a smaller share of the total intermolecular forces.

questions.question:
Methanol can be synthesised from carbon dioxide at high pressure, according to the equation:
$$\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_3OH(g) + H_2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -49 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Justify, using Le Châtelier's principle, why chemists in industry perform this reaction at high pressure.
questions.answer: Le Châtelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, the equilibrium shifts to partially counteract the disturbance. There are 4 mol of gas on the left and 2 mol on the right. Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium to the right, which reduces the number of gas particles and so partially reduces the pressure. This increases the yield of methanol.

questions.question:
Methanol can be synthesised from carbon dioxide at high pressure, according to the equation:
$$\mathrm{CO_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons CH_3OH(g) + H_2O(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -49 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Explain, using collision theory, whether a high or low temperature should be used to produce a high yield of methanol.
questions.answer:
A low temperature should be used.

By collision theory, a reaction happens only when particles collide with enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation. Lowering the temperature lowers the average kinetic energy of the particles, so fewer collisions have energy at or above $E_a$, and both the forward and reverse rates decrease.

The forward reaction is exothermic, so the reverse (endothermic) reaction has the higher activation energy. Lowering the temperature reduces the fraction of successful collisions more for the reaction with the higher $E_a$, so the reverse rate falls by more than the forward rate.

Temporarily rate(forward) > rate(reverse), so the equilibrium shifts to the right until the rates are equal again, giving a higher yield of methanol (though the reaction is slower to reach equilibrium).

questions.question: The percentage ionisation of a 0.102 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of hydrofluoric acid, HF, is 2.53%. Calculate $K_a$ for HF.
For hydrofluoric acid, $K_a = 6.70 \times 10^{-5}$. Calculate the resultant pH when 105 mL of 0.102 mol L$^{-1}$ HF is added to 80.2 mL of 0.104 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH.
questions.answer:
$n(\mathrm{HF}) = 0.105 \times 0.102 = 0.01071$ mol; $n(\mathrm{NaOH}) = 0.0802 \times 0.104 = 0.008341$ mol.

NaOH reacts completely: $n(\mathrm{F^-}) = 0.008341$ mol and $n(\mathrm{HF})$ left $= 0.002369$ mol, in $V = 0.1852$ L:
$[\mathrm{HF}] = 0.01279$ mol L$^{-1}$, $[\mathrm{F^-}] = 0.04504$ mol L$^{-1}$.

This is a buffer. Assuming $x$ is small:
$$[\mathrm{H_3O^+}] = K_a\frac{[\mathrm{HF}]}{[\mathrm{F^-}]} = 6.70 \times 10^{-5} \times \frac{0.01279}{0.04504} = 1.90 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol L}^{-1}$$
$$\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}(1.90 \times 10^{-5}) = 4.72.$$
(Equivalently, $\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{F^-}]}{[\mathrm{HF}]} = 4.174 + 0.547 = 4.72$.)

questions.question:
Iron can be extracted from iron ore, $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$, at very high temperatures:
$$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4(s) + 4C(s) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4CO(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +675.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}, \quad \Delta S = +702.9 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Write an expression for the equilibrium constant for this reaction.
questions.answer: $K_{eq} = [\mathrm{CO}]^4$ (the solids are not included).

questions.question:
Iron can be extracted from iron ore, $\mathrm{Fe_3O_4}$, at very high temperatures:
$$\mathrm{Fe_3O_4(s) + 4C(s) \rightleftharpoons 3Fe(s) + 4CO(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +675.4 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}, \quad \Delta S = +702.9 \text{ J K}^{-1}\text{ mol}^{-1}$$
Using $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$, $\Delta G = +464.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 300 K and $\Delta G = -168.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ at 1200 K. Explain why this reaction is performed at very high temperatures, using the information provided.
questions.answer:
$\Delta H$ is positive (unfavourable) and $\Delta S$ is positive (favourable), so whether the reaction is spontaneous depends on temperature. At low temperature the $\Delta H$ term dominates: at 300 K, $\Delta G = +464.5$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so the reaction is non-spontaneous.

At very high temperature the $-T\Delta S$ term outweighs $\Delta H$: at 1200 K, $\Delta G = -168.1$ kJ mol$^{-1}$, so the forward reaction is spontaneous. Because the reaction is endothermic, a high temperature also increases $K_{eq}$, shifting the equilibrium towards the products so that useful amounts of iron are produced.
